knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multi-DC Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a function on a Cartesian product of convex block domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X:=\prod_{i=1}^k X^i\), where \(X^i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) and \(X\) is Cartesian convex. For \(X^{-i}:=\prod_{j\ne i}X^j\), a function \(h(x^1,\ldots,x^k)\) on \(X\) is multi-DC if, for every block \(i\) and every fixed \(x^{-i}\in X^{-i}\), the function \(h(\cdot,x^{-i})\) is DC on \(X^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a Cartesian convex block domain is multi-DC when, after fixing every block except one, the resulting function of the remaining block is difference-of-convex on that block's domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\;\forall x^{-i}\in X^{-i},\quad h(\cdot,x^{-i})\text{ is DC on }X^i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient DC function classes and directional-derivative closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient conditions for real-valued functions to be DC, and closure of DC functions under pointwise directional differentiation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). Each of the following conditions implies that \(f\) is DC: (i) \(f\) is \(\mathrm{PC}^k\) for some \(k\ge 2\); (ii) \(f\) is \(\varphi\)-weakly convex for an \(\mathrm{LC}^1\) function \(\varphi\); or (iii) \(f\) is lower-\(\mathcal C^2\). Moreover, if \(f\) is DC, then \(f'(\bar x;\cdot)\) is DC for every \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on Euclidean space is DC if it is PC^k for some k at least 2, phi-weakly convex for an LC^1 function phi, or lower-C2. Moreover, for every point, the directional-derivative function of a DC function is itself DC.
assumptions_latex: f\in\mathrm{PC}^k\text{ for some }k\ge 2\;\text{or}\;f\text{ is }\varphi\text{-weakly convex for an }\mathrm{LC}^1\text{ function }\varphi\;\text{or}\;f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^2
\text{For the final assertion, }f\text{ is DC and }\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is DC under each stated sufficient condition; additionally, }f\text{ DC}\implies f'(\bar x;\cdot)\text{ DC for every }\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n.

children.title: Finite-Valued DC Functions
children.top_down_role: Everywhere-finite DC models, their representation scope, plus characteristic structural regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) is finite-valued DC on \(C\), and it is continuous and locally Lipschitz on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, globally finite DC functions on an open convex set.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex. A function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued difference-of-convex (DC) on \(C\) if there exist finite convex functions \(g,h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x)-h(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] The ordered pair \((g,h)\) is a DC decomposition of \(f\). Every such function is continuous and locally Lipschitz on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued DC function is the pointwise difference of two finite convex functions. On an open convex domain, every such function is continuous and locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Valued DC Functions

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector-Lattice Closure of Finite DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure operations for finite-valued DC functions on a common convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=g-h\) and \(u=p-q\), where \(g,h,p,q:C\to\mathbb R\) are convex. Then finite linear combinations of \(f\) and \(u\) are DC, and
\[\max\{f,u\}=\max\{g+q,p+h\}-(h+q),\]
\[\min\{f,u\}=(g+p)-\max\{g+q,p+h\}.\]
Thus the finite-valued DC functions on \(C\) form a vector lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite DC functions are closed under finite linear combinations, pointwise maxima, and pointwise minima, with explicit convex decompositions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha f+\beta u\), \(\max\{f,u\}\), and \(\min\{f,u\}\) are finite-valued DC for all \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vector-Lattice Closure of Finite DC Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Differentiability of Finite DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional derivatives on an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f=g-h\) with finite convex \(g,h\) on an open convex set \(C\), then for every \(x\in C\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[f'(x;d)=g'(x;d)-h'(x;d)\]
exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite DC function is directionally differentiable, with derivative equal to the difference of its component directional derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)\) exists and equals \(g'(x;d)-h'(x;d)\).

notation.meaning: One-sided directional derivative at x in direction d.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Differentiability of Finite DC Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonuniqueness of DC Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-convex-term invariance of finite DC decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f=g-h\) is a finite DC decomposition on \(C\) and \(\varphi:C\to\mathbb R\) is finite convex, then
\[f=(g+\varphi)-(h+\varphi).\]
Thus DC decompositions are generally nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same finite convex function to both components leaves a DC function unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((g+\varphi,h+\varphi)\) is another DC decomposition of \(f\).

notation.meaning: An arbitrary common finite convex summand.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness of DC Decompositions

children.title: Extended-Valued DC Functions
children.top_down_role: DC models incorporating restricted domains or convex constraints through extended values.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Valued DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real DC convention avoiding indeterminate subtraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. An extended-valued function \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is DC if there are a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(g:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and a finite convex function \(h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x)-h(x)\qquad(x\in C).\] This convention makes the subtraction well-defined and yields \(\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{dom}g\). In particular, constraints may be encoded by taking \(g=\widetilde g+\delta_D\) for a convex set \(D\subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-valued DC function subtracts a finite convex function from a proper extended-valued convex function, permitting convex constraints through an indicator.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex and \(h\) is finite convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) is well-defined and \(\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{dom}g\).

notation.meaning: set where the extended-valued function is finite
zero on D and positive infinity outside D

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed asymmetric extended-valued convention is mathematically coherent but is not universal and requires confirmation from the cited source. The constraint example also introduces \(\widetilde g\) without defining its domain or assumptions. Source uncertainty therefore affects the exact definition rather than merely its exposition.

children.title: Effective-Domain Boundary Effects
children.top_down_role: Domain closure, boundary behavior, plus representation limitations specific to extended values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Form of DC First-Order Necessity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone form of the decomposition-based necessary condition at a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=g+\delta_D-h\), where the hypotheses of the Qualified Effective-Domain Sum Rule hold and \(h\) is finite convex on a neighborhood of \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\cap D\). If \(x\) is a local minimizer of \(F\), then \[\partial h(x)\subseteq\partial(g+\delta_D)(x)=\partial g(x)+N_D(x).\] In particular, every \(v\in\partial h(x)\) admits \(v=u+n\) with \(u\in\partial g(x)\) and \(n\in N_D(x)\). At a relative-interior point of \(D\), the normal term vanishes relative to \(\operatorname{aff}D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a qualified boundary local minimizer, subgradients of the subtracted component must be balanced by a convex-component subgradient and a feasible-set normal.
assumptions_latex: The assumptions of Qualified Effective-Domain Sum Rule hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial h(x)\subseteq\partial g(x)+N_D(x)\).

notation.meaning: Decomposition into a component subgradient and a domain normal.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Form of DC First-Order Necessity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of the Unqualified Boundary Sum Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing the need for a convex sum-rule qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), define \[g(x)=\begin{cases}-\sqrt{x},&x\ge0,\\+\infty,&x<0,\end{cases}\qquad D=\{0\}.\] Then \(g\) is proper closed convex, \(\partial g(0)=\varnothing\), and \(N_D(0)=\mathbb R\). But \(g+\delta_D=\delta_{\{0\}}\), so \[\partial(g+\delta_D)(0)=\mathbb R\ne\varnothing=\partial g(0)+N_D(0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a qualification, adding a domain indicator can create boundary subgradients that are absent from the sum of the separate subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(g+\delta_D)(0)\ne\partial g(0)+N_D(0)\).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to \(D\) at zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of the Unqualified Boundary Sum Rule

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualified Effective-Domain Sum Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex subdifferential calculus for an indicator-encoded effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex and let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. If \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\cap\operatorname{ri}D\ne\varnothing,\] then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\cap D\), \[\operatorname{dom}(g+\delta_D)=\operatorname{dom}g\cap D,\qquad \partial(g+\delta_D)(x)=\partial g(x)+N_D(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior qualification, encoding a convex domain adds its normal cone exactly to the convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(g+\delta_D)(x)=\partial g(x)+N_D(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\cap D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Effective-Domain Sum Rule
Effective-Domain Boundary Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary behavior for DC models containing a convex-domain indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(g\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex, and let \(h\) be finite convex near \(D\). For \(f=g+\delta_D-h\), one has \(\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{dom}g\cap D\). If \(x\in\operatorname{dom}g\cap\operatorname{bdry}D\) and the convex subdifferential sum rule is qualified, then \[\partial(g+\delta_D)(x)=\partial g(x)+N_D(x).\] Thus boundary normals enter first-order DC stationarity, whereas \(N_D(x)=\{0\}\) at interior points of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding a convex domain adds its normal cone to the convex subdifferential at boundary points, changing DC stationarity relative to interior points.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex and \(h\) is finite convex near \(D\).
The convex subdifferential sum rule is qualified at the boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(g+\delta_D)(x)=\partial g(x)+N_D(x)\) at qualified boundary points.

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to D at x

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domain identity is correct, but saying that the sum rule is 'qualified' does not state an inspectable mathematical hypothesis, such as an appropriate relative-interior condition. The cited DC section is not confirmed to support the exact subdifferential sum rule and boundary-stationarity claim.

children.title: Local DC Representability
children.top_down_role: DC representations valid on neighborhoods or restricted regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Local DC Representability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise-neighborhood definition on an open Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is locally DC on \(U\) if, for every \(\bar x\in U\), there exist an open convex neighborhood \(V_{\bar x}\subseteq U\) and finite convex functions \(g_{\bar x},h_{\bar x}:V_{\bar x}\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \[f(x)=g_{\bar x}(x)-h_{\bar x}(x)\qquad(x\in V_{\bar x}).\] The decomposition may depend on \(\bar x\); no compatibility between decompositions on overlapping neighborhoods is included in the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is locally DC when every point has a neighborhood on which the function is a difference of two finite convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is locally DC precisely when such a neighborhood decomposition exists at every point of \(U\).

notation.meaning: convex neighborhood associated with the point

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Regularity of Locally DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity inherited from finite convex components on each neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is locally DC on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable throughout \(U\). Whenever \(f=g-h\) on a neighborhood of \(x\), with finite convex \(g,h\), \[f'(x;d)=g'(x;d)-h'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial g(x)}(d)-\sigma_{\partial h(x)}(d)\] for every direction \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally DC function is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable, with its directional derivative represented by any local convex component pair.
assumptions_latex: A finite convex-difference representation exists on a neighborhood of every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Regularity of Locally DC Functions

children.title: Global DC Representability
children.top_down_role: Single DC representations valid across the full domain of interest.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is globally DC on \(C\) exactly when one pair of finite convex functions \((g,h)\) represents it throughout \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-decomposition definition over the entire prescribed convex domain.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is globally DC on \(C\) if there exists one pair of finite convex functions \(g,h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x)-h(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] The same convex components must therefore be valid throughout \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global DC representability requires one pair of finite convex functions whose difference equals the given function throughout the prescribed convex domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Global DC Representability

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Algebra of Global DC Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operations preserving a single finite convex-difference representation over the prescribed domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_k=g_k-h_k\) be globally DC on the same convex set \(C\), with finite convex \(g_k,h_k\). Every finite linear combination \(\sum_k\lambda_k f_k\) is globally DC after assigning each signed component to the appropriate convex sum. Finite maxima and minima are also globally DC. In particular, \[\max\{f_1,f_2\}=\max\{g_1+h_2,g_2+h_1\}-(h_1+h_2),\] finite maxima follow inductively, and \(\min_k f_k=-\max_k(-f_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global DC functions on one convex domain are closed under finite linear combinations, maxima, and minima, with explicit full-domain decompositions.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_k\) has finite convex components valid throughout \(C\).
Only finitely many functions are combined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\lambda_k f_k\), \(\max_k f_k\), and \(\min_k f_k\) are globally DC on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Real coefficient in the finite linear combination.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Algebra of Global DC Representations

children.title: Local-to-Global Extension Barriers
children.top_down_role: Obstructions preventing local DC structure from extending to a global representation.

assumptions_latex: Any proposed extension is required to be finite-valued and DC on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no finite-valued DC function \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(F|_{(0,infty)}=f\).

notation.meaning: restriction of F to the positive half-line

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite-valued DC extension beyond an open domain.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(f(x)=1/x\). The function \(f\) is convex, and hence DC, on \((0,\infty)\), but there is no finite-valued DC function \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(F(x)=f(x)\) for every \(x>0\). Thus \(f\) is a boundary-blow-up counterexample to extension from its open domain to the ambient real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function 1/x is DC on the positive half-line but has no finite-valued DC extension to the real line; it is a boundary-blow-up extension counterexample.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Extension Barriers

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Boundary Trace Is Necessary for DC Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary continuity condition at a boundary point added to the extension domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\bar x\in\overline D\), and suppose \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) has a finite-valued DC extension \(F\) to an open neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Then \[\lim_{x\to\bar x,\ x\in D}f(x)=F(\bar x).\] Hence absence of a finite path-independent boundary limit, including boundary blow-up, precludes such an extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite DC extension forces a finite boundary trace; blow-up or incompatible boundary limits obstruct extension.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is finite-valued and DC on an open neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\to F(\bar x)\) as \(x\to\bar x\) through \(D\).

notation.meaning: Boundary point included in the proposed extension domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Boundary Trace Is Necessary for DC Extension

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Boundary Trace Is Not Sufficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional derivative-variation obstruction to DC extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:(0,1)\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)\). It is smooth, hence locally DC, on \((0,1)\), and has the continuous extension \(f(0)=0\). Nevertheless it has no finite DC extension to any open interval containing \(0\): \[f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x)\] has infinite total variation on every \((0,\varepsilon)\), whereas a one-dimensional DC function has one-sided derivatives of locally bounded variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous, even Lipschitz, boundary behavior need not suffice for DC extension when derivative variation accumulates infinitely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite DC function on a neighborhood of \(0\) restricts to \(f\) on \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Boundary Trace Is Not Sufficient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: B-Stationarity Implies Local Minimality in a Piecewise-Affine DC Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency of B-stationarity for a convex composite objective over piecewise-affine DC inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}, where every g_i and h_i is convex piecewise affine. Let f=\varphi\circ\psi, with \varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} convex and \psi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} piecewise affine. Every B\text{-stationary solution of }\min_{x\in X}f(x)\text{ is a local minimizer.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a problem whose constraints are differences of convex piecewise-affine functions and whose objective is a convex univariate function composed with a piecewise-affine function, every B-stationary feasible solution is locally minimizing.
assumptions_latex: g_i,h_i\text{ are convex piecewise affine for all }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is a local minimizer of }f\text{ on }X.

children.title: Piecewise-Affine DC Functions
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral piecewise-affine DC structure across finite cell decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous piecewise-affine functions on finite polyhedral partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and affine on every cell of a finite polyhedral partition of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Then there are finite families of affine functions \(a_i(x)=p_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i\) and \(b_j(x)=q_j^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_j\) such that \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le r}a_i(x)-\max_{1\le j\le s}b_j(x).\] Both maxima are finite polyhedral convex functions; consequently every continuous finite piecewise-affine function is globally DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous finite piecewise-affine function admits a difference-of-two finite maxima of affine functions and is therefore globally DC.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is affine on each cell of a finite polyhedral partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\max_i a_i-\max_j b_j\), so \(f\) is globally DC.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.1 Piecewise affine functions p. 185
I.* Piecewise Linear Functions p. 67

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.1 Piecewise affine functions p. 185
I.* Piecewise Linear Functions p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity Is Necessary for Finite DC Representability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for finite piecewise-affine functions on the full Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite piecewise-affine function with a jump discontinuity cannot equal \(g-h\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) for finite convex \(g,h\), because every such difference is continuous. For example,
\[f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0,\\1,&x\ge0\end{cases}\]
is piecewise affine but is not finite-valued DC on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discontinuous piecewise-affine function need not be DC; the one-dimensional step function is a canonical counterexample.
assumptions_latex: Any proposed DC components would be finite convex functions on the full ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Jump-discontinuous piecewise-affine functions are not finite-valued DC on the full space.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuity Is Necessary for Finite DC Representability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative from Active Diff-Max Pieces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional calculus for a difference of finite affine maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le r}(p_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i)-\max_{1\le j\le s}(q_j^{\mathsf T}x+\beta_j).\]
If \(I(x)\) and \(J(x)\) are the active sets of the two maxima, then
\[f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}p_i^{\mathsf T}d-\max_{j\in J(x)}q_j^{\mathsf T}d.\]
Moreover, \(f\) is globally Lipschitz with constant \(\max_i\|p_i\|+\max_j\|q_j\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active affine slopes determine the directional derivative, and the diff-max representation supplies a global Lipschitz bound.
assumptions_latex: Both maxima contain finitely many affine functions.
\(I(x)\) and \(J(x)\) are their active index sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed directional-derivative formula and Lipschitz bound hold.

notation.meaning: Active affine indices in the two convex maxima.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Derivative from Active Diff-Max Pieces

children.title: Piecewise Linear-Quadratic DC Functions
children.top_down_role: Piecewise linear-quadratic DC structure across quadratic regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Linear-Quadratic DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous piecewise linear-quadratic members of the DC class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is a piecewise linear-quadratic DC function if there is a finite polyhedral partition \(\{P_k\}_{k=1}^m\) and coefficients \(Q_k=Q_k^{\mathsf T}\), \(c_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(d_k\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_kx+c_k^{\mathsf T}x+d_k\qquad(x\in P_k),\] the formulas agree on common cell boundaries, and \(f=g-h\) for some finite convex functions \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). No individual matrix \(Q_k\) is required to be positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise linear-quadratic DC function is continuous, quadratic-affine on finitely many polyhedral cells, and globally representable as a difference of finite convex functions.
assumptions_latex: \(\{P_k\}_{k=1}^m\) is a finite polyhedral partition of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
The quadratic-affine cell formulas agree on shared boundaries.
A global finite convex decomposition \(f=g-h\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) belongs simultaneously to the continuous piecewise linear-quadratic and globally DC classes.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.2 Piecewise linear-quadratic functions p. 198

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.2 Piecewise linear-quadratic functions p. 198

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Regularity of Continuous PLQ Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity inherited from finitely many consistent quadratic pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite continuous piecewise linear-quadratic function on a finite polyhedral partition is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable. If \(x+td\) lies for all sufficiently small \(t>0\) in a cell having formula \(q_k\), then
\[f'(x;d)=\nabla q_k(x)^{\mathsf T}d.\]
When the ray lies in a shared face, agreement of the regional formulas makes the tangential value independent of the adjacent formula chosen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous finite PLQ functions are locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable, with the derivative supplied by the quadratic piece entered by the direction.
assumptions_latex: The representation uses finitely many polyhedral cells.
The quadratic-affine formulas agree on overlaps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and \(f'(x;d)\) exists for every \(x,d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Regularity of Continuous PLQ Functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Automatic DC Representability of Continuous Finite PLQ Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globally finite continuous functions on finite polyhedral partitions of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and quadratic-affine on every cell of a finite polyhedral partition of \(\mathbb R^n\), then there exist finite convex piecewise linear-quadratic functions \(g,h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[f=g-h.\]
Thus DC membership is automatic under these global finiteness, continuity, and finite-partition hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every globally finite continuous piecewise linear-quadratic function on a finite polyhedral partition is a difference of two convex PLQ functions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is quadratic-affine on each cell of a finite polyhedral partition of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) for finite convex PLQ functions \(g,h\).
knowledge_statements.title: Automatic DC Representability of Continuous Finite PLQ Functions

children.title: Piecewise-Class Representation Transitions
children.top_down_role: Changes in decomposition geometry when moving between affine or quadratic pieces.

assumptions_latex: Piecewise-affine and piecewise linear-quadratic classes use continuous cellwise formulas on finite polyhedral partitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{PA}_{\mathrm{DC}}\subsetneq\mathrm{PLQ}_{\mathrm{DC}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict transition from piecewise-affine to piecewise linear-quadratic DC structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under finite polyhedral partitions with continuous cellwise formulas, every piecewise-affine DC function is a piecewise linear-quadratic DC function. The containment is strict. The function \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=x^2\) belongs to the piecewise linear-quadratic DC class but not to the piecewise-affine class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The piecewise-affine DC class is a strict subclass of the piecewise linear-quadratic DC class, with the convex quadratic x squared witnessing strictness.

children.title: Difference-of-Maxima DC Functions
children.top_down_role: DC functions represented through differences of finite or structured maxima.

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Maxima DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite diff-max representation with convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex. Suppose \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\) and \(v_1,\ldots,v_s\) are finite convex functions on \(C\). Then \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le r}u_i(x)-\max_{1\le j\le s}v_j(x)\] is DC on \(C\), because each finite maximum is convex. When all \(u_i\) and \(v_j\) are affine, this specializes to the standard difference-of-max-affine representation of continuous piecewise-affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A difference of two finite maxima of convex functions is DC; affine components give the standard piecewise-affine diff-max form.
assumptions_latex: The families \(\{u_i\}_{i=1}^r\) and \(\{v_j\}_{j=1}^s\) are finite and consist of finite convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\max_i u_i-\max_j v_j\) is DC on \(C\).

notation.meaning: convex components of the positive maximum
convex components of the negative maximum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Component Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional formula for finite diff-max representations at relative-interior points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(u_i,v_j\) be finite convex functions on \(C\). Define \(I(x)=\arg\max_i u_i(x)\) and \(J(x)=\arg\max_j v_j(x)\). Then, for every \(d\in\operatorname{par}C\), \[ f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}u_i'(x;d)-\max_{j\in J(x)}v_j'(x;d),\qquad f=\max_i u_i-\max_j v_j. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative of a finite diff-max function is the difference of the directional maxima over its active positive and negative components.
assumptions_latex: The two families are finite and consist of finite convex functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}u_i'(x;d)-\max_{j\in J(x)}v_j'(x;d)\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{par}C\).

notation.meaning: Active index sets of the positive and negative maxima.
Linear space parallel to the affine hull of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Component Directional Derivative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Finite Max–Min Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise lattice identities specific to a finite difference of maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite real-valued families \(\{u_i\}_{i=1}^r\) and \(\{v_j\}_{j=1}^s\), \[ \max_i u_i(x)-\max_j v_j(x)=\min_j\max_i\bigl(u_i(x)-v_j(x)\bigr)=\max_i\min_j\bigl(u_i(x)-v_j(x)\bigr). \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite difference of maxima equals both the associated min–max and max–min arrays of pairwise differences.
assumptions_latex: All displayed component values are finite at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i u_i-\max_j v_j=\min_j\max_i(u_i-v_j)=\max_i\min_j(u_i-v_j)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Finite Max–Min Forms

children.title: Composite DC Functions
children.top_down_role: DC structure arising from admissible outer-inner compositions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q=\Phi\circ F\) is a composite DC function exactly when \(q=G-H\) on \(C\) for some finite convex functions \(G,H:C\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued DC functions presented through an outer function and a vector-valued inner map.

source_refs.locator: 6.1.3 Difference-of-convex composite with diff-max p. 335

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):C\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(\Phi:D\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(F(C)\subseteq D\). A function \(q:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is a composite DC function relative to \((\Phi,F)\) if \(q(x)=\Phi(F(x))\) for every \(x\in C\) and there exist finite convex functions \(G,H:C\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \[q(x)=G(x)-H(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite DC function is a composition of an outer function with a vector-valued inner map that also admits a global difference-of-finite-convex decomposition on the prescribed convex domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite DC Functions

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1.3 Difference-of-convex composite with diff-max p. 335

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Decomposition of Fractional Powers of Positive Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for a fractional power of a smooth positive convex function to admit a quadratic DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R_{++}\) be a \(C^2\) convex function, let \(p\in(0,1)\), and let \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex. If \(x\mapsto \nabla f(x)/f(x)^{1-p/2}\) is bounded on \(\mathcal O\), then for some \(\lambda>0\), \(f(x)^p=[\lambda x^\top x+f(x)^p]-\lambda x^\top x\) is a dc decomposition on \(\mathcal O\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a positive twice continuously differentiable convex function has bounded gradient after the stated scaling, then each power between zero and one is DC on the open convex set and has the displayed quadratic decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\lambda>0:\ f(x)^p=[\lambda x^\top x+f(x)^p]-\lambda x^\top x\text{ is dc on }\mathcal O\)

children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where composition preserves or loses a usable DC representation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite linear combinations, finite pointwise maxima, finite pointwise minima, and the displayed diff-max affine outer compositions of \(f_1,ldots,f_m\) are DC on \(C\).

notation.meaning: coefficient vectors of the affine outer pieces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary sufficient regimes preserving finite-valued DC structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(m,r,s\) be positive integers, and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite-valued DC functions. For every \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\in\mathbb{R}\), the function \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i\) is DC on \(C\); finite pointwise maxima and minima of DC functions are also DC on \(C\). Moreover, for vectors \(a_k,b_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and scalars \(\alpha_k,\beta_\ell\in\mathbb{R}\), define \[\Phi(z)=\max_{1\le k\le r}(a_k^{\mathsf T}z+\alpha_k)-\max_{1\le\ell\le s}(b_\ell^{\mathsf T}z+\beta_\ell).\] Then \(x\mapsto\Phi(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\) is DC on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite linear combinations, finite pointwise maxima, finite pointwise minima, and finite difference-of-max-affine outer compositions preserve finite-valued DC structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Representation Closure Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary Outer Composition Does Not Preserve DC Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary showing that an unrestricted outer function can destroy finite-valued DC regularity even with an affine inner map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be the affine DC map \(F(x)=x\), and define
\[
\Phi(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t\in\mathbb Q,\\0,&t\notin\mathbb Q.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\Phi\circ F=\Phi\) is discontinuous at every point. Since every finite-valued DC function on an open interval is continuous, \(\Phi\circ F\) is not DC on any nonempty open interval. Thus arbitrary outer composition does not preserve DC structure, even for an affine inner map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrestricted discontinuous outer function can produce a non-DC composition even when the inner map is affine.
assumptions_latex: \Phi(t)=1\text{ on }\mathbb Q\text{ and }\Phi(t)=0\text{ on }\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is affine and DC, but }\Phi\circ F\text{ is not DC on any nonempty open interval}.
knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Outer Composition Does Not Preserve DC Structure

children.title: Matrix DC Functions
children.top_down_role: DC functions whose arguments or structured variables are matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real matrix spaces with the Frobenius inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be nonempty and convex. A function \(F:C\to\mathbb R\) is a matrix DC function on \(C\) if there exist proper convex functions \(G,H:C\to\mathbb R\) such that \[F(X)=G(X)-H(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in C.\] The ordered pair \((G,H)\) is called a DC decomposition of \(F\). Convexity is taken with respect to the vector-space structure of \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), equivalently after vectorizing the matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued matrix function is DC when it is the pointwise difference of two proper convex functions on a convex matrix domain.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=G-H\) for some proper convex functions \(G,H:C\to\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Frobenius inner product on the matrix space.
An ordered DC decomposition of the matrix function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic finite-dimensional regularity already owned by the finite-valued DC leaf.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix DC functions inherit ordinary finite-dimensional DC regularity after vectorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable.

children.title: Spectral DC Functions
children.top_down_role: Orthogonally or unitarily invariant DC functions induced by spectral data.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant DC decompositions on symmetric or rectangular matrix spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix function \(F:C\to\mathbb R\) on an invariant convex set \(C\) is spectral DC if it has a DC decomposition \(F=G-H\) whose convex components possess the same matrix invariance as \(F\). For symmetric matrices this means \(G(QXQ^{\mathsf T})=G(X)\) and \(H(QXQ^{\mathsf T})=H(X)\) for every orthogonal \(Q\). For rectangular matrices it means invariance under \(X\mapsto UXV^{\mathsf T}\) for compatible orthogonal \(U,V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral DC function has convex difference components that retain its orthogonal similarity or left-right orthogonal invariance.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and invariant under the applicable orthogonal action.
\(F:C\to\mathbb R\) is invariant under that action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=G-H\) with invariant proper convex functions \(G\) and \(H\).

notation.meaning: Invariant convex components of the DC decomposition.

children.title: Eigenvalue-Based DC Functions
children.top_down_role: DC constructions organized through ordered eigenvalue mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordered Eigenvalues as Differences of Ky Fan Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical DC decompositions of individual ordered eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda_1(X)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(X)\) and \(S_k(X)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)\), with \(S_0=0\). Then
\[\lambda_k(X)=S_k(X)-S_{k-1}(X),\qquad k=1,\ldots,n.\]
Since every \(S_k\) is convex, every ordered eigenvalue is finite-valued DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every ordered eigenvalue is DC because it is the difference of consecutive convex Ky Fan eigenvalue sums.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_k=S_k-S_{k-1}\) is DC for every \(k\).

notation.meaning: Sum of the k largest eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Eigenvalues as Differences of Ky Fan Sums

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Formula for Ky Fan Eigenvalue Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support representation for sums of the largest eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) and \(1\le k\le n\),
\[S_k(X):=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)=\max\{\langle X,P\rangle_F:0\preceq P\preceq I,\ \operatorname{tr}P=k\}.\]
Consequently, \(S_k\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of the k largest eigenvalues is a support function over a compact spectrahedron and is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_k\) has the displayed variational representation and is convex.

notation.meaning: Both P and I-P are positive semidefinite.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational Formula for Ky Fan Eigenvalue Sums
Eigenvalue-Based DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral lifts on real symmetric matrices using ordered eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) be convex and invariant under orthogonal similarity, and let \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb R^n\) list the eigenvalues of \(X\) in nonincreasing order. If \(\phi_1,\phi_2:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are convex and permutation-invariant, then their spectral lifts \(G(X)=\phi_1(\lambda(X))\) and \(H(X)=\phi_2(\lambda(X))\) are convex. Consequently, \[F(X)=\phi_1(\lambda(X))-\phi_2(\lambda(X))=G(X)-H(X)\] is an eigenvalue-based DC function on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A difference of convex symmetric functions of the ordered eigenvalues lifts to a DC function on symmetric matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) is convex and orthogonally invariant.
\(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) are finite convex permutation-invariant functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=(\phi_1\circ\lambda)-(\phi_2\circ\lambda)\) is DC on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Vector of eigenvalues of X in nonincreasing order.

children.title: Singular-Value-Based DC Functions
children.top_down_role: DC constructions organized through singular-value mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix Rank Is Not Finite-Valued DC on the Full Matrix Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity boundary separating rank from finite singular-value DC constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rank function is discontinuous at every rank-deficient matrix that is a limit of matrices of larger rank. Since every finite-valued DC function on the open space \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is continuous, \(X\mapsto\operatorname{rank}X\) is not finite-valued DC on the full matrix space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix rank is not finite DC on the full matrix space because it is discontinuous at rank-deficient matrices.
assumptions_latex: The domain is all of \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(\cdot)\) has no decomposition into two finite convex functions on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Rank Is Not Finite-Valued DC on the Full Matrix Space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordered Singular Values as Differences of Ky Fan Norms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical DC decompositions of individual ordered singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\sigma_1(X)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r(X)\ge0\), where \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), and define \(K_k(X)=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i(X)\), with \(K_0=0\). Every \(K_k\) is a convex unitarily invariant norm, and
\[\sigma_k(X)=K_k(X)-K_{k-1}(X).\]
Thus every ordered singular value is finite-valued DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each ordered singular value is the difference of two consecutive convex Ky Fan norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_k=K_k-K_{k-1}\) is DC for \(k=1,\ldots,r\).

notation.meaning: Ky Fan k-norm, the sum of the k largest singular values.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Singular Values as Differences of Ky Fan Norms
Singular-Value-Based DC Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unitarily invariant lifts on real rectangular matrix spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be convex and invariant under left-right orthogonal transformations, and let \(\sigma(X)\in\mathbb R^r\), where \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), list the singular values in nonincreasing order. If \(\psi_1,\psi_2:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\) are convex and absolutely symmetric, then \(G(X)=\psi_1(\sigma(X))\) and \(H(X)=\psi_2(\sigma(X))\) are convex. Hence \[F(X)=\psi_1(\sigma(X))-\psi_2(\sigma(X))\] is a singular-value-based DC function on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A difference of convex absolutely symmetric functions of singular values lifts to a DC function on rectangular matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is convex and left-right orthogonally invariant.
\(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\) are finite convex absolutely symmetric functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=(\psi_1\circ\sigma)-(\psi_2\circ\sigma)\) is DC on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Vector of singular values of X in nonincreasing order.
Number of singular values in the vector.

children.title: DC Decomposition Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of convex-component pairs representing the same DC function.

knowledge_statements.title: DC Decomposition Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common convex perturbations generate multiple decompositions of one DC function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f=g-h\) on \(C\), where \(g\) and \(h\) are proper convex functions finite on \(C\). For every convex function \(q:C\to\mathbb R\), \[f=(g+q)-(h+q).\] Thus a DC decomposition is generally nonunique. If \(C\) contains more than one point, the choices \(q_\alpha(x)=\alpha\|x\|^2\) for \(\alpha\ge 0\) give a continuum of decompositions, although some pairs may coincide under exceptional component identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same convex function to both components preserves their difference, usually producing infinitely many DC decompositions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(f=g-h\) with proper convex components finite on \(C\).

notation.meaning: A common convex perturbation of both components.

knowledge_statements.title: DC Decomposition Equivalence Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise equivalence of ordered convex component pairs on a fixed domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a convex set \(C\). For ordered pairs \((g_1,h_1)\) and \((g_2,h_2)\) of finite convex functions on \(C\), define \[(g_1,h_1)\sim(g_2,h_2)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_1-h_1=g_2-h_2\ \text{on }C.\] Equivalently, \(g_1+h_2=g_2+h_1\) pointwise on \(C\). This relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; its equivalence class consists precisely of all DC decompositions representing the same function on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two ordered convex pairs are equivalent exactly when their pointwise differences define the same function on the fixed domain.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb R\) are finite convex functions for \(i\in\{1,2\}\).

children.title: Decomposition-Dependent Algorithmic Behavior
children.top_down_role: Effects of equivalent decomposition choices on subproblems, criticality, or numerical behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Decompositions with Different DCA Dynamics and Criticality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit one-dimensional examples separating update dynamics, convergence behavior, and component-based criticality across equivalent decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(C=\mathbb R\), let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2\). The equivalent decompositions
\[
(g,h)=\left(\tfrac12x^2,0\right),\qquad (\widetilde g,\widetilde h)=\left(x^2,\tfrac12x^2\right)
\]
give, from the same \(x^k\), the unique basic DCA updates
\[
x^{k+1}=0\quad\text{and}\quad x^{k+1}=\tfrac12x^k,
\]
respectively. Hence one representative reaches the minimizer in one update, whereas the other converges geometrically when \(x^0\neq0\). Separately, for \(f(x)=x\), the equivalent pairs
\[
(g,h)=(x,0),\qquad (\widehat g,\widehat h)=(x+|x|,|x|)
\]
have different component-criticality behavior at zero:
\[
\partial g(0)\cap\partial h(0)=\varnothing,
\qquad
\partial\widehat g(0)\cap\partial\widehat h(0)=[0,1]\neq\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent one-dimensional decompositions can produce one-step versus geometric DCA convergence and can disagree on component-based criticality.
assumptions_latex: \text{The basic DCA update uses an arbitrary }y^k\in\partial h(x^k)\text{ followed by exact minimization of the convex subproblem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{DCA iterates, convergence behavior, and component-criticality are not invariants of the represented objective alone}
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Decompositions with Different DCA Dynamics and Criticality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representative Dependence of the Basic DCA Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of the set-valued basic DCA step on the selected representative of one DC-decomposition equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a selected decomposition \(f=g-h\) on a closed convex set \(C\), define the basic DCA update map
\[
T_{g,h}(x):=\bigcup_{y\in\partial h(x)}\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\{g(z)-\langle y,z\rangle\}.
\]
If \(f=\widetilde g-\widetilde h\) is an equivalent decomposition, equality of the represented objectives does not imply
\[
\partial h(x)=\partial\widetilde h(x),\qquad T_{g,h}(x)=T_{\widetilde g,\widetilde h}(x),
\]
or equality of the component-based critical sets \(\{x:\partial g(x)\cap\partial h(x)\neq\varnothing\}\) and \(\{x:\partial\widetilde g(x)\cap\partial\widetilde h(x)\neq\varnothing\}\). Thus the basic update and component-criticality test are properties of the chosen ordered pair, not solely of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent DC decompositions can have different negative-component subgradients, DCA update maps, and component-based critical sets.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
g,h,\widetilde g,\widetilde h\text{ are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions}
g-h=\widetilde g-\widetilde h\text{ wherever the displayed differences are finite}
\partial h(x)\neq\varnothing\text{ and the displayed convex subproblems attain their minima at points under consideration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{g,h}\text{ and }\{x:\partial g(x)\cap\partial h(x)\neq\varnothing\}\text{ need not be invariant under equivalent DC decompositions}

notation.meaning: Set-valued basic DCA update map associated with the ordered convex pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Component Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC decompositions allowing genuine nonsmoothness in both convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. A nonsmooth-component DC decomposition of \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is an identity \(f=g-h\) with proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions \(g,h:C\to\mathbb R\), where neither component is differentiable throughout \(\operatorname{ri}C\). At a point \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), componentwise first-order information is represented by the convex subdifferentials \(\partial g(x)\) and \(\partial h(x)\); these sets can remain non-singleton even when cancellation makes \(f\) differentiable at \(x\).

assumptions_latex: \(g,h\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions finite on \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) with both \(g\) and \(h\) nondifferentiable somewhere in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Regularity Component Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC decompositions with one smooth and one genuinely nonsmooth convex component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex. A mixed-regularity DC decomposition of \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is an identity \[f=g-h\] in which \(g,h:U\to\mathbb R\) are convex, exactly one component is continuously differentiable on \(U\), and the other fails to be differentiable at some point of \(U\). knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Component Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous quadratic strengthening of both components in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f=g-h\) on \(C\), with finite convex functions \(g,h\). For any \(\rho>0\), define \[g_\rho(x)=g(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2,\qquad h_\rho(x)=h(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2.\] Then \(g_\rho\) and \(h_\rho\) are \(\rho\)-strongly convex under the convention that \(u\) is \(\rho\)-strongly convex when \(u-\rho\|\cdot\|^2/2\) is convex, and \(f=g_\rho-h_\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same positive quadratic to both convex components yields an equivalent decomposition with both components strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g_\rho-h_\rho\), and both \(g_\rho\) and \(h_\rho\) are \(\rho\)-strongly convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Component Strong Convexity Does Not Transfer to the Difference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of inferring objective curvature from the component moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho>0\), let \[g(x)=\frac{\rho}{2}x^2,\qquad h(x)=\frac{\rho+1}{2}x^2.\] The components are respectively \(\rho\)- and \((\rho+1)\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R\), but \(g(x)-h(x)=-x^2/2\) is strictly concave and unbounded below. children.top_down_role: Redistribution of common convex structure across a DC component pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Transfer Between Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of a DC decomposition under common convex additions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and suppose \(f=g-h\) on \(C\), where \(g,h:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions with intersecting effective domains. For every finite-valued convex function \(q:C\to\mathbb{R}\), one has
\[
f=(g+q)-(h+q)\quad\text{on }C.
\]
Both \(g+q\) and \(h+q\) are convex. Thus any convex term may be transferred simultaneously to the two components without changing the represented DC function or its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same finite convex function to both components preserves their difference and yields another valid DC decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Convexification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean quadratic DC representation of a weakly convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A proper function \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex, for \(\rho\geq0\), precisely when
\[
g(x):=f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2
\]
is convex on \(C\). In that case \(h(x):=\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\) is convex and
\[
f(x)=g(x)-h(x),\qquad x\in C,
\]
so quadratic convexification supplies an explicit DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly convex function becomes convex after adding a sufficiently large quadratic, producing an explicit DC decomposition by subtracting that quadratic.

children.title: Convexification Curvature Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Curvature regimes governing whether quadratic modification yields usable convex components.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Curvature Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hessian criterion for the least quadratic convexification parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. For \(\rho\geq0\), the function \(x\mapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\) is convex on \(U\) if and only if
\[
\nabla^2 f(x)+\rho I\succeq0\quad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
Consequently, the sharp uniform threshold is
\[
\rho_*:=\max\left\{0,\sup_{x\in U}-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\right\},
\]
with the convention that no finite quadratic convexification exists when this supremum is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic convexification succeeds exactly when the added curvature offsets every negative Hessian eigenvalue; the worst negative eigenvalue determines the threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f+(\rho/2)\lVert\cdot\rVert^2\text{ is convex}\iff \nabla^2f(x)+\rho I\succeq0\ \forall x\in U

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions such that \(D:=C\cap\operatorname{dom}g\cap\operatorname{dom}h\neq\varnothing\). A convex-constrained DC program has the form
\[
\inf_{x\in D}\{g(x)-h(x)\}.
\]
If \(\delta_C\) denotes the convex indicator of \(C\) and \(\widetilde g:=g+\delta_C\), then the same program can be written as
\[
\inf_{x\in\operatorname{dom}\widetilde g\cap\operatorname{dom}h}\{\widetilde g(x)-h(x)\}.
\]
Thus the explicit convex constraint is absorbed into the first convex component, with the common effective domain retained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Inequalities Can Define a Nonconvex Feasible Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary separating DC-constrained programs from convex-constrained DC programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\mathbb R\), \(g_1(x)=1\), and \(h_1(x)=x^2\). Both components are finite convex functions, but
\[
\{x\in\mathbb R:g_1(x)-h_1(x)\leq0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty),
\]
which is nonconvex. Thus convexity of the components of a DC inequality does not imply convexity of its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The DC inequality 1 minus x squared less than or equal to zero has convex components but defines two disjoint rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:g_1(x)-h_1(x)\leq0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\text{ is nonconvex}
knowledge_statements.title: DC Inequalities Can Define a Nonconvex Feasible Set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Violation Feasibility Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar feasibility certificate for finitely many finite-valued DC inequalities on a common convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(g_i,h_i:D\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex functions for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define
\[
V(x)=\max\{0,g_1(x)-h_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x)-h_m(x)\}.
\]
Then \(V\) is finite-valued and DC on \(D\), \(V\ge0\), and
\[
V(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum positive violation of finitely many DC inequalities is DC and vanishes exactly on their common feasible set.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}.
g_i,h_i:D\to\mathbb R\text{ are finite convex functions for }i=1,\ldots,m.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V\text{ is DC on }D\quad\text{and}\quad V^{-1}(0)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in D:g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Violation Feasibility Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Epigraph Reformulation of the Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent epigraph form for a finite-valued DC objective subject to finitely many DC inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f_i=g_i-h_i\) be finite-valued DC functions on \(D\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), and consider
\[\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\}.\]
Its epigraph reformulation is
\[\inf_{(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R}\{t:g_0(x)-h_0(x)-t\le0,\ g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\}.\]
The programs have the same infimal value. If an optimal solution exists, \((x^*,t^*)\) is optimal in the lifted problem if and only if \(x^*\) is optimal in the original problem and \(t^*=f_0(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued DC objective can be moved into one additional DC inequality using an epigraph variable without changing optimal values or minimizers.
assumptions_latex: The original feasible set is nonempty for the minimizer correspondence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization with DC objective and finitely many DC inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finitely constrained DC program is
\[
\inf_{x\in C}\{g_0(x)-h_0(x):g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\},

where \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex and every \(g_i,h_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex on a common region containing the feasible points. knowledge_statements.title: Composite DC Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maximum composite of DC component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A finite max-composite DC program is
\[
\inf_{x\in C}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{g_i(x)-h_i(x)\},
\]
where each \(g_i,h_i:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex and every displayed difference is finite on the region of interest. The outer function is the coordinatewise maximum, applied to the vector of DC component values. This class is itself DC because the finite maximum admits an explicit convex-difference reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite DC program minimizes the finite maximum of DC component functions; the maximum can itself be rewritten as one convex difference.
assumptions_latex: g_i-h_i\text{ is finite on the region of interest}

knowledge_statements.title: Diff-Max DC Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC programs represented as a difference of finite convex maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A diff-max DC program on a nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has objective
\[
F(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq p}G_i(x)-\max_{1\leq j\leq q}H_j(x),
\]
and minimizes \(F\) over \(C\), where every \(G_i,H_j:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex and both maxima are finite on the region of interest. Since a finite pointwise maximum of convex functions is convex, the two displayed maxima form a valid DC decomposition of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diff-max program minimizes one finite maximum of convex functions minus another, which directly supplies its DC decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \max_iG_i\text{ and }\max_jH_j\text{ are finite on the region of interest}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=\max_{1\leq i\leq p}G_i-\max_{1\leq j\leq q}H_j\text{ is DC on }C

children.title: Composite-to-Diff-Max Reformulations

knowledge_statements.title: Composite-to-Diff-Max Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of a finite maximum of DC functions into diff-max form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For proper convex functions \(g_i,h_i:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), with all quantities finite at the point considered, define \(H:=\sum_{k=1}^m h_k\). Then
\[
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{g_i(x)-h_i(x)\}
=
\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\left\{g_i(x)+\sum_{k\neq i}h_k(x)\right\}-H(x).
\]
Each function inside the maximum is convex, and \(H\) is convex. Hence a finite max-composite of DC functions has a diff-max representation, with the second maximum taken over the singleton family \(\{H\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding all negative components gives an exact identity that rewrites a maximum of DC functions as a difference of convex maxima.
assumptions_latex: \text{all terms are finite at the point considered}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_i(g_i-h_i)=\max_i\left(g_i+\sum_{k\neq i}h_k\right)-\sum_kh_k

notation.meaning: Aggregate convex function formed by summing all negative components.

children.title: Separable DC Programs

knowledge_statements.title: Separable DC Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC minimization with independent variable blocks and separable component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) be nonempty convex sets. A separable DC program has the form
\[
\inf_{x_i\in X_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m}\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(g_i(x_i)-h_i(x_i)\bigr),
\]
where each \(g_i,h_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex. On the product space \(X:=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\), the aggregate functions \(G(x):=\sum_i g_i(x_i)\) and \(H(x):=\sum_i h_i(x_i)\) are convex, so the objective equals \(G-H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable DC program sums DC terms depending on disjoint variable blocks; summing positive and negative components gives the aggregate decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^m(g_i(x_i)-h_i(x_i))=G(x)-H(x)

notation.meaning: Aggregate convex components on the product space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Structured Learning via Statistics and Optimization p. 111

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Structured Learning via Statistics and Optimization p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupled Feasibility Destroys Independent Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for exact independent-block optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1(x_1)=(x_1-1)^2\) and \(f_2(x_2)=(x_2+1)^2\). Their independent minimizers are \(1\) and \(-1\). Under the coupled constraint \(x_1=x_2\), this pair is infeasible and
\[
\min_{x_1=x_2}\bigl(f_1(x_1)+f_2(x_2)\bigr)=2
\]
is attained at \((0,0)\), whereas \(\min f_1+\min f_2=0\). Thus additive objective separability does not imply independent optimization unless the feasible set also factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupling constraint can invalidate independent block minimization even when the objective is additively separable.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Feasibility Destroys Independent Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Product Decomposition of Values and Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization decomposition for a separable DC objective over a Cartesian-product effective feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(D_i\neq\varnothing\), let \(f_i=g_i-h_i:D_i\to\mathbb R\), and suppose \(\alpha_i:=\inf_{x_i\in D_i}f_i(x_i)\in\mathbb R\). Define
\[
D:=\prod_{i=1}^mD_i,\qquad F(x_1,\ldots,x_m):=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i).
\]
Then
\[
\inf_{x\in D}F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i,
\qquad
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}F(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in D_i}f_i(x_i).
\]
Consequently, the full program has a minimizer if and only if every component program has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over a Cartesian product, the optimal value of a separable DC program is the sum of its component values and its minimizer set is the product of the component minimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_DF=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_D F=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname*{argmin}_{D_i}f_i

notation.meaning: Effective feasible domain of component i.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Product Decomposition of Values and Minimizers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical or deterministic finite-sum objective with DC summands and an explicit common effective domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(m\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}\), and let \(g_i,h_i:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Assume
\[
D:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g_i\cap\operatorname{dom}h_i\bigr)\neq\varnothing.
\]
A finite-sum DC program is
\[
\inf_{x\in D}F(x),\qquad F(x):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(g_i(x)-h_i(x)\bigr).
\]
Defining \(G:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i\) and \(H:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m h_i\) gives proper convex aggregate components and \(F=G-H\) on \(D\). Omitting the positive normalization factor does not change the program class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-sum DC program averages DC terms sharing one variable on their nonempty common effective domain; averaging the positive and negative components gives the aggregate decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum DC Programs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC minimization with terms depending on possibly overlapping variable blocks.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Structured Learning via Statistics and Optimization p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B,m\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}\), let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_B)\) range over a nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\prod_{b=1}^B\mathbb{R}^{n_b}\), and let \(S_i\subseteq\{1,\ldots,B\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). For each \(i\), let \(g_i,h_i:\prod_{b\in S_i}\mathbb{R}^{n_b}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, and assume
\[
D:=\{x\in C:x_{S_i}\in\operatorname{dom}g_i\cap\operatorname{dom}h_i\text{ for every }i\}\neq\varnothing.
\]
A block-structured DC program is
\[
\inf_{x\in D}F(x),\qquad F(x):=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(g_i(x_{S_i})-h_i(x_{S_i})\bigr).
\]
The sets \(S_i\) may overlap. Lifting each component to the product space and summing produces proper convex functions \(G\) and \(H\) such that \(F=G-H\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-structured DC program minimizes a sum of DC terms involving selected, possibly overlapping variable blocks on their common effective domain; lifting and summing the components gives a global DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Structured DC Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic DC program is an optimization problem whose random objective admits an integrable pointwise convex decomposition. Specifically, it has the form \[\min_{x\in X}\mathbb E[g(x,\omega)-h(x,\omega)].\] Under the stated assumptions, expectation preserves convexity, so \(G(x)=\mathbb E[g(x,\omega)]\) and \(H(x)=\mathbb E[h(x,\omega)]\) are convex on their common effective domain. children.title: Expectation-Based DC Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Cancellation Does Not Justify Component Expectations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between an integrable random DC difference and a valid difference of expected convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z:\Omega\to[0,+\infty)\) be measurable with \(\mathbb E Z=+\infty\), and define \[g(x,\omega)=Z(\omega)+x^2,\qquad h(x,\omega)=Z(\omega).\] For every \(\omega\), both functions are finite and convex in \(x\), and \(g(x,\omega)-h(x,\omega)=x^2\). Hence \(\mathbb E[g(x,\omega)-h(x,\omega)]=x^2\), but \(\mathbb E g(x,\omega)=\mathbb E h(x,\omega)=+\infty\), so \(\mathbb E g-\mathbb E h\) is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable pointwise DC difference need not equal a difference of component expectations when both convex components have infinite expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E(g-h)(x)=x^2\), while \(\mathbb E g(x)-\mathbb E h(x)\) is undefined.

children.title: Sample-Average DC Programs
children.top_down_role: Finite-sample surrogates for expectation-based DC formulations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform SAA Consistency for DC Component Averages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure uniform component and objective convergence, value convergence, and argmin consistency on a compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(\omega_1,\omega_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. For every \(x\in X\), assume \(g(x,\cdot)\) and \(h(x,\cdot)\) are measurable, while \(g(\cdot,\omega)\) and \(h(\cdot,\omega)\) are continuous and convex on \(X\) almost surely. Suppose a measurable \(K\ge0\) and \(x_0\in X\) satisfy
\[
|g(x,\omega)-g(y,\omega)|+|h(x,\omega)-h(y,\omega)|\le K(\omega)\|x-y\|,
\]
\(\mathbb E K<\infty\), and \(\mathbb E[|g(x_0,\omega)|+|h(x_0,\omega)|]<\infty\). Define \(G=\mathbb Eg\), \(H=\mathbb Eh\), \(F=G-H\), and their sample averages \(G_N,H_N,F_N=G_N-H_N\). Then, almost surely,
\[
\sup_X|G_N-G|\to0,\qquad \sup_X|H_N-H|\to0,\qquad \sup_X|F_N-F|\to0.
\]
Consequently \(\min_XF_N\to\min_XF\); if \(F_N(x_N)\le\inf_XF_N+\varepsilon_N\) and \(\varepsilon_N\to0\), every accumulation point of \((x_N)\) lies in \(\operatorname*{argmin}_XF\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable random Lipschitz bound on a compact domain gives almost-sure uniform convergence of both empirical convex components and their DC difference, with value and approximate-minimizer consistency.
assumptions_latex: X\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and compact}.
g(x,\cdot),h(x,\cdot)\text{ are measurable for every }x\in X.
g(\cdot,\omega),h(\cdot,\omega)\text{ are continuous and convex on }X\text{ almost surely}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|G_N-G\|_\infty,\|H_N-H\|_\infty,\|F_N-F\|_\infty\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}0,\quad\inf_XF_N\to\inf_XF,\quad\operatorname{Limsup}\operatorname*{argmin}_{\varepsilon_N}F_N\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_XF.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform SAA Consistency for DC Component Averages

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Mean-Square Sampling Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-decision mean-square law for independent sample averages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\), and let \(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_N\) be i.i.d. If \(q(x,\omega)=g(x,\omega)-h(x,\omega)\) has finite variance and \[F_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Nq(x,\omega_i),\qquad F(x)=\mathbb E q(x,\omega),\] then \[\mathbb E|F_N(x)-F(x)|^2=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(q(x,\omega))}{N}.\] Thus the fixed-decision root-mean-square error is \(\operatorname{sd}(q(x,\omega))/\sqrt N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For i.i.d. samples, the pointwise SAA objective has exact one-over-N mean-square error and one-over-square-root-N root-mean-square error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E|F_N(x)-F(x)|^2=\operatorname{Var}(q(x,\omega))/N\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\), and let \(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_N\) have the same marginal law. If \(g(x,\omega)\) and \(h(x,\omega)\) are integrable, define \[G_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ng(x,\omega_i),\quad H_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Nh(x,\omega_i),\quad F_N(x)=G_N(x)-H_N(x).\] Then \[\mathbb E G_N(x)=G(x),\qquad \mathbb E H_N(x)=H(x),\qquad \mathbb E F_N(x)=F(x),\] where \(G=\mathbb E g\), \(H=\mathbb E h\), and \(F=G-H\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) can be written as a difference \(q=p-r\) of two finite sublinear functions if and only if there are nonempty compact convex sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) such that \(q=\sigma_A-\sigma_B\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sum and product rules for quasidifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the sign-dependent scalar action on quasidifferential pairs to encode all four product sign cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be quasidifferentiable at \(x\). Then \(f_1+f_2\) and \(f_1f_2\) are quasidifferentiable at \(x\), and \[\mathcal D(f_1+f_2)(x)=\mathcal Df_1(x)+\mathcal Df_2(x),\qquad \mathcal D(f_1f_2)(x)=f_1(x)\mathcal Df_2(x)+f_2(x)\mathcal Df_1(x).\] Pair addition is componentwise, and for \(\mathcal Df=[A,B]\), scalar multiplication is \(c[A,B]=[cA,cB]\) when \(c\ge0\) and \(c[A,B]=[cB,cA]\) when \(c\le0\). Thus the latter identity yields the stated four sign-dependent formulas for the sub- and superdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum and product of two functions quasidifferentiable at the same point are quasidifferentiable there. Quasidifferentials add componentwise, while the product obeys the ordinary product rule with negative scalar multiplication interchanging the sub- and superdifferential components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal D(f_1+f_2)(x)=\mathcal Df_1(x)+\mathcal Df_2(x),\qquad \mathcal D(f_1f_2)(x)=f_1(x)\mathcal Df_2(x)+f_2(x)\mathcal Df_1(x)
