children.title: KL Descent Framework
children.top_down_role: Descent geometry used in KL-based analysis of DCA trajectories.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Descent Gives Square-Summable Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The complete descent-only consequence owned by this component leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F(x^{k+1})+a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2\leq F(x^k)\) for every \(k\), where \(a>0\), and \(\inf_kF(x^k)>-\infty\), then \[a\sum_{k=0}^{N}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2\leq F(x^0)-F(x^{N+1})\] for every \(N\). Consequently, \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2<\infty\) and \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform sufficient descent and a lower objective bound make squared step lengths summable and steps vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient Descent Gives Square-Summable Steps

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper lower semicontinuous and has the KL property at every cluster point.
\((x^k)\) is bounded and satisfies sufficient decrease with constant \(a>0\).
A relative-error bound holds with constant \(b>0\), together with subsequential value continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<+\infty\), and \(x^k\to\bar x\) with \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-dimensional KL convergence framework applicable to DCA trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x^k)\) be bounded and suppose
\[
F(x^{k+1})+a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2\leq F(x^k),
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|
\]
for constants \(a,b>0\). Assume some subsequence \(x^{k_j}\to\bar x\) satisfies \(F(x^{k_j})\to F(\bar x)\), and that \(F\) has the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property at every cluster point. Then the trajectory has finite length,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<+\infty,
\]
and the whole sequence converges to a critical point \(\bar x\) satisfying \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sufficient decrease, relative error, value continuity, boundedness, and the KL property force finite trajectory length and convergence to one critical point.
knowledge_statements.title: KL Descent Framework

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract finite-dimensional KL theorem is plausible and appropriately classified, but its exact sufficient-decrease, relative-error, continuity, and KL hypotheses require an authoritative theorem citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Relative-Error Framework
children.top_down_role: Relative-error controls connecting trajectory progress to criticality measures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact DCA Verification under a Lipschitz Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical verification of abstract relative error for exact DCA with a smooth subtracted component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=g-h\), where \(g\) is proper closed convex and \(h\) is convex and differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on a region containing consecutive iterates. Suppose exact DCA chooses \(x^{k+1}\) so that \(
abla h(x^k)\in\partial g(x^{k+1})\). Then \[w^{k+1}:=
abla h(x^k)-
abla h(x^{k+1})\in\partial F(x^{k+1})\] and \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq\|w^{k+1}\|\leq L\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For exact DCA, Lipschitz continuity of the subtracted component's gradient converts subproblem optimality into relative error.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex, differentiable, and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on the relevant region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq L\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\).

notation.meaning: DCA stationarity residual at the new iterate
Lipschitz constant of the gradient of h

knowledge_statements.title: Exact DCA Verification under a Lipschitz Gradient
Relative-Error Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract relative-error condition for KL analysis of DCA-type sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x^k)_{k\geq0}\subset\operatorname{dom}F\). The sequence satisfies a relative-error condition if there exist \(b>0\) and \(w^{k+1}\in\partial F(x^{k+1})\) such that \[\|w^{k+1}\|\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\quad\text{for every }k\geq0.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\). Thus the stationarity residual is controlled by the most recent DCA displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DCA sequence satisfies relative error when each new stationarity residual is bounded by a constant times its latest step length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\) for every \(k\geq0\).

notation.meaning: stationarity residual at the new iterate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no source supports the precise limiting-subdifferential formulation or its use in KL-based DCA analysis.

children.title: Framework Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility conditions linking descent geometry to relative-error control.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compatibility Conditions for KL Descent-Error Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally owned interface conditions; the finite-length and single-point conclusions belong to their dedicated theorem leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sufficient-descent and relative-error components are KL-compatible along \((x^k)\) when they concern the same proper lower-semicontinuous objective \(F\), the residual is evaluated at the new iterate \(x^{k+1}\), both estimates use uniform constants, the bounded trajectory has subsequential value continuity, and \(F\) has the KL property on its cluster set. Concretely, for some \(a,b>0\), \[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\geq a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatibility requires the descent and residual estimates to align on one objective, one step, uniform constants, compatible limiting values, and a KL cluster set.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and lower semicontinuous and \((x^k)\subset\operatorname{dom}F\) is bounded.
The displayed inequalities hold for the same objective and displacement with constants independent of \(k\).
Objective values are continuous along convergent subsequences and \(F\) is KL on the cluster set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The descent and relative-error estimates can be combined through a uniformized KL inequality on the cluster set.
knowledge_statements.title: Compatibility Conditions for KL Descent-Error Calculus
Framework Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility conditions joining descent, relative error, continuity, and the KL property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x^k)\) be bounded. Suppose that for some \(a,b>0\), \[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\geq a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.\] Assume every convergent subsequence \((x^{k_j})\) satisfies \(F(x^{k_j})\to F(\bar x)\), where \(x^{k_j}\to\bar x\), and that \(F\) has the KL property on the cluster set. Then the descent and relative-error estimates enter the same KL inequality and imply finite trajectory length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Descent and relative error are KL-compatible when bounded iterates also have objective continuity along convergent subsequences and KL regularity on their cluster set.
assumptions_latex: \((x^k)\) is bounded and satisfies the displayed descent and relative-error inequalities.
\(F\) has the KL property on the cluster set of \((x^k)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the compatibility leaf, but the finite-length conclusion is a nontrivial abstract KL theorem and has no cited source supporting the exact hypotheses.

children.title: Inexactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Error regimes where the combined KL framework ceases to support its intended conclusions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Summable Descent Errors Need Not Ensure Finite Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between summability of additive descent errors and the stronger control needed for trajectory length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(a>0\), let \(F\equiv0\) on \(\mathbb R\), and set \(x^k=\sin(\log(k+1))\), \(\varepsilon_k=a|x^{k+1}-x^k|^2\), and \(\eta_k=0\). Then \((x^k)\) is bounded, \(F\) is KL, and \[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\geq a|x^{k+1}-x^k|^2-\varepsilon_k,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b|x^{k+1}-x^k|+\eta_k.\] Moreover, \(\sum_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\), but \(\sum_k|x^{k+1}-x^k|=\infty\) and \((x^k)\) does not converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even summable additive descent errors can permit a bounded nonconvergent trajectory of infinite length when they pay only for squared steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\varepsilon_k<\infty\), yet \(\sum_k|x^{k+1}-x^k|=\infty\) and \((x^k)\) does not converge.
knowledge_statements.title: Summable Descent Errors Need Not Ensure Finite Length
Inexactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-summable descent errors can destroy finite length and iterate convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the perturbed descent requirement \[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\geq a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2-\varepsilon_k\] together with \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|+\eta_k\). Summability assumptions cannot generally be discarded: take \(F\equiv0\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), \(x^k=(-1)^k\), \(\varepsilon_k=4a\), and \(\eta_k=0\). Both inequalities hold, and \(F\) is a KL function, but \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|=2\); hence the trajectory has infinite length and the iterates do not converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant objective with alternating iterates satisfies sufficiently large non-summable error inequalities but has infinite length and no iterate limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|=+\infty\) and \((x^k)\) does not converge.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Length Consequence of the Quantified KL Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-length conclusion only; construction of the component inequalities and subsequent rate refinements belong to siblings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x^k)\subset\operatorname{dom}F\) be bounded. Suppose that for constants \(a,b>0\), \[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\geq a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.\] Assume some subsequence \(x^{k_j}\to\bar x\) satisfies \(F(x^{k_j})\to F(\bar x)\), and \(F\) has the KL property at every cluster point. Then \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<+\infty.\] Consequently, every tail length \(\sum_{k=N}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\) is finite and tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quantified descent, relative error, subsequential value continuity, boundedness, and KL regularity imply finite total trajectory length.
assumptions_latex: \((x^k)\) is bounded and satisfies the displayed descent and relative-error inequalities with uniform positive constants.
A convergent subsequence has objective values converging to the objective at its limit.
\(F\) has the KL property at every cluster point.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Length Consequence of the Quantified KL Framework
Finite-Length DCA Trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-length conclusion from the abstract KL descent-relative-error mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \((x^k)\) be a bounded DCA trajectory. Suppose it satisfies uniform sufficient descent and relative error, objective values are continuous along its convergent subsequences, and \(F\) has the KL property at every cluster point. Then \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<+\infty.\] Consequently, for every \(N\geq0\), the remaining travel distance \(\sum_{k=N}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\) is finite and tends to zero as \(N\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded DCA trajectory satisfying compatible descent, relative error, continuity, and KL assumptions has finite total length.
assumptions_latex: \((x^k)\) satisfies uniform sufficient descent and relative error.
\(F\) is continuous along convergent subsequences of \((x^k)\).
\(F\) has the KL property at every cluster point.

notation.meaning: DC objective monitored along the trajectory

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem matches the leaf, but the phrases “uniform sufficient descent” and “relative error” are not expanded into quantified inequalities, and no source establishes that the stated assumptions suffice for finite length.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Point Convergence of DCA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of the whole finite-length trajectory to one critical point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. If a bounded DCA trajectory \((x^k)\) has finite length and satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\), then \((x^k)\) is Cauchy and converges to a single point \(\bar x\). If additionally the graph of \(\partial F\) is sequentially closed along \((x^{k+1},w^{k+1})\), with \(w^{k+1}\in\partial F(x^{k+1})\) and \(w^{k+1}\to0\), then \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite length makes the entire DCA sequence converge to one point; closedness of the subdifferential graph makes that limit critical.
assumptions_latex: The relative-error condition holds with a uniform constant \(b>0\).
The limiting-subdifferential graph is sequentially closed along the residual sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\to\bar x\) and \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Finite length correctly implies single-point convergence, but the criticality conclusion requires a clearly specified subgradient selection converging to zero and an applicable closed-graph result. The exact DCA hypotheses need a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteration Complexity Induced by KL-Exponent Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-to-accuracy form of the standard local KL-exponent rate trichotomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the rate hypotheses and exponent convention of the KL-exponent theorem, let \(r_k:=F(x^k)-F(\bar x)\). For \(0<\theta\leq\tfrac12\), geometric convergence gives \(r_k\leq\varepsilon\) and \(\|x^k-\bar x\|\leq\varepsilon\) after \(O(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) iterations in the local regime. For \(\tfrac12<\theta<1\), \[r_k=O\!\left(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)}\right),\qquad \|x^k-\bar x\|=O\!\left(k^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)}\right),\] so the corresponding iteration bounds are \[k=O\!\left(\varepsilon^{-(2\theta-1)}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad k=O\!\left(\varepsilon^{-(2\theta-1)/(1-\theta)}\right),\] respectively. The case \(\theta=0\) terminates finitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometric and polynomial KL rates translate into logarithmic or explicit power-law iteration bounds for objective and iterate accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The compatible descent-relative-error framework yields convergence to \(\bar x\).
The local KL inequality uses exponent \(\theta\in[0,1)\).
The asymptotic regime has been entered and \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration-to-accuracy bounds are logarithmic for \(0<\theta\leq1/2\), polynomial with the displayed exponents for \(1/2<\theta<1\), and finite for \(\theta=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Complexity Induced by KL-Exponent Rates
KL-Exponent Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard asymptotic rates under a KL exponent and descent-relative-error estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the hypotheses yielding \(x^k\to\bar x\), and set \(r_k=F(x^k)-F(\bar x)\). Suppose locally \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\geq c(F(x)-F(\bar x))^{\theta}\), where \(c>0\) and \(\theta\in[0,1)\). Then: if \(\theta=0\), termination occurs in finitely many steps; if \(0<\theta\leq\tfrac12\), both \(r_k\) and \(\|x^k-\bar x\|\) converge geometrically; if \(\tfrac12<\theta<1\), \[r_k=O\!\left(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)}\right),\qquad \|x^k-\bar x\|=O\!\left(k^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KL exponent separates finite termination, geometric convergence, and explicit polynomial objective and iterate rates.
assumptions_latex: The trajectory satisfies uniform sufficient descent and relative error.
The displayed KL inequality holds locally with exponent \(\theta\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trajectory obeys the finite, geometric, or polynomial rate regime specified by \(\theta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the rate-regime leaf, but the exact objective and iterate rates, including the geometric regime and exponent convention, require an authoritative KL rate theorem.

children.title: Subanalytic Regimes
children.top_down_role: KL analysis specialized to subanalytic DC data.

knowledge_statements.title: Subanalytic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL regularity supplied by subanalytic geometry in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, with subanalytic graph, and assume \(F\) is continuous on its domain near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\). Then \(F\) satisfies the KL property at \(\bar x\): there exist \(\eta>0\), a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and a concave function \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb{R}_+\), continuous at zero and \(C^1\) on \((0,\eta)\), such that \[\varphi'(F(x)-F(\bar x))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\geq1\] whenever \(x\in U\) and \(0<F(x)-F(\bar x)<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous subanalytic objective, with suitable domain continuity, satisfies a local KL inequality at each subdifferentiable point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and has a subanalytic graph.
\(F\) is continuous on its domain near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has the KL property at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: neighborhood on which the KL inequality holds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the subanalytic-regime leaf, but the precise graph-subanalyticity and domain-continuity assumptions under which the extended-real-valued KL theorem holds require an authoritative source.

children.title: Semialgebraic Regimes
children.top_down_role: KL analysis specialized to semialgebraic DC data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semialgebraic Extended-Real Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph definition for semialgebraic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set is semialgebraic when it is a finite union of sets described by finitely many polynomial equalities and inequalities. A proper function \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is semialgebraic when \(\operatorname{epi}F\) is semialgebraic; equivalently, \(\operatorname{dom}F\) and \(\operatorname{gph}(F|_{\operatorname{dom}F})\) are semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real objective is semialgebraic through its epigraph, equivalently through its finite-valued graph and domain.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and never takes the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}F\text{ is semialgebraic}\iff \operatorname{dom}F\text{ and }\operatorname{gph}(F|_{\operatorname{dom}F})\text{ are semialgebraic}.
knowledge_statements.title: Semialgebraic Extended-Real Objective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semialgebraic DC Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of finite-valued semialgebraic DC data under subtraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g,h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are semialgebraic, then \(g-h\) is semialgebraic. Finite sums, products, maxima, and minima of finite-valued semialgebraic functions are likewise semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-valued semialgebraic functions are closed under subtraction and the other elementary finite operations used to assemble DC objectives.
assumptions_latex: All displayed functions are finite-valued and semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g-h\text{ is semialgebraic}.
knowledge_statements.title: Semialgebraic DC Closure
Semialgebraic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semialgebraic objectives automatically furnish KL regularity for DCA analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and suppose its epigraph is semialgebraic. Then \(F\) is a KL function: at every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\), there exist \(c>0\), \(\eta>0\), a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and an exponent \(\theta\in[0,1)\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\geq c\bigl(F(x)-F(\bar x)\bigr)^\theta\] for all \(x\in U\) satisfying \(0<F(x)-F(\bar x)<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper lower-semicontinuous semialgebraic objective has a local power-form KL inequality at each subdifferentiable point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) satisfies a power-form KL inequality at \(\bar x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property and power-form KL statement are standard for semialgebraic objectives, but no citation supports the exact extended-real-valued formulation and exponent range.

children.title: Definable Regimes
children.top_down_role: KL analysis in broader definable geometric settings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Definable Extended-Real Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definability relative to one fixed o-minimal expansion of the real field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an o-minimal structure \(\mathcal S\). A proper function \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is \(\mathcal S\)-definable when its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,r):F(x)\le r\}\) is \(\mathcal S\)-definable. Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dom}F\) and the graph of \(F|_{\operatorname{dom}F}\) are \(\mathcal S\)-definable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real objective is definable when its epigraph, equivalently its finite-valued graph over its domain, is definable in one fixed o-minimal structure.
assumptions_latex: A fixed o-minimal structure \(\mathcal S\) is chosen.
\(F\) is proper and never takes the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}F\text{ is }\mathcal S\text{-definable}\iff \operatorname{gph}(F|_{\operatorname{dom}F})\text{ and }\operatorname{dom}F\text{ are }\mathcal S\text{-definable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Definable Extended-Real Objective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Definable DC Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of definability from finite-valued DC components to their objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g,h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are definable in the same o-minimal structure \(\mathcal S\), then \(F=g-h\) is \(\mathcal S\)-definable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The difference of two finite-valued functions definable in the same structure is definable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g-h\text{ is }\mathcal S\text{-definable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Definable DC Closure
Definable Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL regularity for objectives definable in a fixed o-minimal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an o-minimal structure on \((\mathbb{R},+ ,\cdot)\). Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous with definable epigraph. Then \(F") is a KL function: for each \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\), there exist \(\eta>0\), a neighborhood \(U\), and a definable concave desingularizing function \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb{R}_+\) such that \[\varphi'(F(x)-F(\bar x))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\geq1\] whenever \(x\in U\) and \(0<F(x)-F(\bar x)<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous objective definable in an o-minimal structure satisfies the KL property at every subdifferentiable point.
assumptions_latex: A fixed o-minimal expansion of the real field is given.
\(F\) is proper and lower semicontinuous with definable epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has the KL property at \(\bar x\) with a definable desingularizing function.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement contains the malformed text “F\")” and does not explicitly state the usual continuity, differentiability, and normalization properties of the desingularizing function. An authoritative o-minimal KL source is also required before choosing the exact formulation.

children.title: Tame-Geometry Inclusion Relations
children.top_down_role: Navigation among overlapping or nested tame-geometry classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Subanalyticity Does Not Imply Global Subanalyticity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for an unqualified subanalytic-to-\(\mathbb R_{\mathrm{an}}\)-definable inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph \(G=\{(x,e^x):x\in\mathbb R\}\) is semianalytic locally and hence subanalytic, because locally it is the zero set of the real-analytic function \((x,y)\mapsto y-e^x\). It is not globally subanalytic and therefore is not definable in \(\mathbb R_{\mathrm{an}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential graph is locally subanalytic but not globally subanalytic, so arbitrary subanalytic sets cannot be identified with the globally subanalytic o-minimal class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is subanalytic but not globally subanalytic}.

notation.meaning: graph of the real exponential function
o-minimal structure generated by restricted analytic functions

knowledge_statements.title: Local Subanalyticity Does Not Imply Global Subanalyticity
Tame-Geometry Inclusion Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precise inclusions among semialgebraic, globally subanalytic, and definable classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every semialgebraic subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is definable in the semialgebraic o-minimal structure and in every o-minimal expansion of the real field. Every globally subanalytic set is definable in \(\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an}}\), the o-minimal structure generated by restricted analytic functions. Hence semialgebraic and globally subanalytic objectives are special cases of definable objectives after choosing the corresponding structure. Locally subanalytic sets need not be globally subanalytic, so the unqualified inclusion of all subanalytic sets in \(\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an}}\) is not valid without a boundedness or global-subanalyticity qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semialgebraic and globally subanalytic objects are definable in suitable o-minimal structures, while arbitrary locally subanalytic objects require a global qualification.
assumptions_latex: All sets and functions are finite-dimensional.
Definability is interpreted relative to the stated o-minimal structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{semialgebraic}\subset\text{definable}\) and \(\text{globally subanalytic}\subset\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an}}\text{-definable}\).

notation.meaning: o-minimal structure of globally subanalytic sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusion distinctions are mathematically plausible and fit the leaf, but the claims about semialgebraic, globally subanalytic, and locally subanalytic classes have no cited tame-geometry source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Length and Iterate Convergence in the Linear Error-Bound Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of local objective contraction and sufficient descent after neighborhood entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that for all \(k\ge k_0\), \(\Delta_k:=F(x^k)-F_*\ge0\), \(\Delta_{k+1}\le q\Delta_k\) with \(q\in(0,1)\), and \[\Delta_k-01\Delta_{k+1}\ge a\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert^2\] with \(a>0\). Then \[\sum_{k=k_0}^{\infty}\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\le\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{k_0}/a}}{1-01\sqrt q}<\infty.\] Consequently, \((x^k)\) converges to some \(\bar x\), and \[\lVert x^k-01\bar x\rVert\le\frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{k_0}/a}}{1-01\sqrt q}\,q^{(k-k_0)/2}.\] If the accompanying closedness or cluster-criticality assumptions identify all cluster points with the critical set \(S\), then \(\bar x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Q-linear objective convergence plus quadratic descent gives finite trajectory length and R-linear convergence of iterates to a critical point.
assumptions_latex: Cluster points are critical for the final membership conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{k=k_0}^{\infty}\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert<\infty,\qquad \lVert x^k-01\bar x\rVert=O(q^{k/2}).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Length and Iterate Convergence in the Linear Error-Bound Regime
Local Error-Bound DCA Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence from residual error bounds plus quadratic objective growth control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^k)\) be a DCA trajectory converging to a critical set \(S\) on which \(F=F_*\). Suppose eventually \[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\geq a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,\quad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|,\] and, locally, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\) and \(F(x)-F_*\leq M\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\). Then \[F(x^{k+1})-F_*\leq q\bigl(F(x^k)-F_*\bigr),\qquad q=\frac{Mb^2\kappa^2}{a+Mb^2\kappa^2}<1.\] Thus the objective residual converges Q-linearly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local stationarity error bound and quadratic upper growth convert DCA descent and relative error into Q-linear objective convergence.
assumptions_latex: Uniform sufficient descent and relative error hold eventually.

notation.meaning: local critical set at objective level F_*

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed contraction follows algebraically once all inequalities apply at the relevant late iterates, but the theorem does not precisely state those locality and neighborhood-entry conditions, and no DCA error-bound source supports the result.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Subregularity DCA Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric subregularity of the stationarity mapping along a local DCA regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, let \(S=(\partial F)^{-1}(0)\), and let \(\bar x\in S\). The stationarity mapping \(\partial F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] A DCA trajectory enters this regime once all sufficiently late iterates lie in \(U\), allowing relative-error estimates to control their distance to the critical set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity bounds distance to the critical set by the stationarity residual near a reference critical point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,(\partial F)^{-1}(0))\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\) locally around \(\bar x\).

source_refs.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

source_witnesses.locator: H.* Metric Descriptions of Convergence p. 181

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric Subregularity Does Not Isolate a Critical Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between metric and strong metric subregularity for a stationarity mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(F(x,y)=\tfrac12x^2\). Then \(\partial F(x,y)=\{(x,0)\}\) and \[S=(\partial F)^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R.\] For every \((x,y)\), \[\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)=|x|=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x,y)),\] so \(\partial F\) is metrically subregular with modulus one at every \(((0,y),0)\). Nevertheless, no point of \(S\) is locally isolated, so strong metric subregularity fails there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity may hold exactly when the critical set is a continuum; it does not imply isolated criticality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial F\text{ is metrically subregular at every }((0,y),0)\text{ but not strongly metrically subregular there}.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity Does Not Isolate a Critical Point

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposition Dependence of the DC PL Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single objective with two DC decompositions producing different criticality residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2+x\), so \(f_*=-1/4\). With the decomposition \(g_1=f\), \(h_1=0\), the residual is \(r_1(x)=|2x+1|\) and \(f(x)-f_*=r_1(x)^2/4\). With \(g_2(x)=x^2+x+|x|\) and \(h_2(x)=|x|\), both components are convex and \(g_2-h_2=f\), but at \(x=0\), \[\partial g_2(0)=[0,2],\qquad \partial h_2(0)=[-1,1],\qquad r_2(0)=0,\] while \(f(0)-f_*=1/4\). Thus a positive-constant DC PL inequality holds globally for the first decomposition but cannot hold on any region containing \(0\) for the second.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same objective can satisfy the DC PL inequality for one decomposition and fail it for another.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Dependence of the DC PL Residual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Objective Convergence under a DC PL Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective contraction obtained by combining a DC PL residual inequality with sufficient descent and relative error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_k:=f(x^k)-f_*\ge0\) and \(r(x):=\operatorname{dist}(\partial g(x),\partial h(x))\). Suppose all relevant iterates lie in a region where \(\Delta(x)\le r(x)^2/(2\mu)\), and suppose \[\Delta_k-\Delta_{k+1}\ge a\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert^2,\qquad r(x^{k+1})\le b\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\] with \(a,01\mu>0\) and \(b\ge0\). Then \[\Delta_{k+1}\le q\Delta_k,\qquad q=\frac{b^2}{2a\mu+b^2}<1.\] Hence \(\Delta_k\le q^{k-k_0}\Delta_{k_0}\) while the trajectory remains in the regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC PL inequality, sufficient descent, and relative error yield geometric contraction of objective gaps.
assumptions_latex: \(f=g-h\) satisfies \(f(x)-f_*\le r(x)^2/(2\mu)\) on the relevant region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_{k+1}\le\frac{b^2}{2a\mu+b^2}\Delta_k.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Objective Convergence under a DC PL Inequality

assumptions_latex: \(f=g-h\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(g,h\) are proper closed convex functions and \(f_*:=\inf f> -\infty\).
The criticality residual \(r(x):=\operatorname{dist}(\partial g(x),\partial h(x))\) is finite on the stated region \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f_*\le r(x)^2/(2\mu)\) for every \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: distance between the two convex subdifferentials
region on which the regime holds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth DC PL condition expressed through the decomposition-dependent criticality residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A DC Polyak–Łojasiewicz regime with constant \(\mu>0\) holds on \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}g\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) when
\[
f(x)-f_*\le \frac{1}{2\mu}\operatorname{dist}^{2}\!\bigl(\partial g(x),\partial h(x)\bigr)
\quad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
Here the distance between two sets is the infimum of pairwise distances. The condition is global when \(U=\operatorname{dom}f\), and local when \(U\) is a neighborhood of a specified solution set or critical point. Because the residual depends on the chosen DC decomposition, the regime is a property of \((g,h)\), not merely of the pointwise function \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC PL regime bounds objective suboptimality by the squared distance between the convex subdifferentials of the two DC components.
knowledge_statements.title: DC Polyak–Łojasiewicz Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but no inspectable source supports this decomposition-dependent DC PL convention or its normalization.

children.title: Relative Strong Convexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: DCA convergence settings governed by relative strong convexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent Nonsmooth Subgradient Selections Are Too Strong
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating the convex-difference convention from an inequality quantified over every independent pair of reference and objective subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\omega(x)=|x|\) and \(f(x)=\mu|x|\) on \(\mathbb R\), where \(\mu>0\). Then \(f-\mu\omega\equiv0\) is convex. At \(x=0\), however, choose \(v=\mu\in\partial f(0)\) and \(s=-1\in\partial\omega(0)\). For \(y>0\), \[f(y)<f(0)+v(y-0)+\mu D_\omega^s(y,0).\] Hence convexity of \(f-\mu\omega\) does not justify quantifying the generalized Bregman inequality over every independent \(v\in\partial f(x)\) and \(s\in\partial\omega(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsmooth reference, convexity of f−μω does not imply the Bregman inequality for every independently selected pair of subgradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The every-\(v\), every-\(s\) nonsmooth formulation is strictly stronger than convexity of \(f-\mu\omega\).

notation.meaning: generalized Bregman divergence for the selected reference subgradient

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Nonsmooth Subgradient Selections Are Too Strong

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Difference Characterization with a Differentiable Reference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent formulation under the standard differentiable-reference convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and let \(\omega:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable. For \(\mu>0\), \(f-\mu\omega\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(v\in\partial f(x)\), \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\mu D_\omega(y,x),\qquad D_\omega(y,x):=\omega(y)-\omega(x)-\langle\nabla\omega(x),y-x\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a differentiable convex reference, relative strong convexity is equivalent to convexity of f minus μ times the reference.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite convex and \(\omega\) is finite, convex, and differentiable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex relative to \(\omega\) if and only if \(f-\mu\omega\) is convex on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the differentiable reference

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Difference Characterization with a Differentiable Reference
Relative Strong Convexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient-based relative strong convexity, suitable for nonsmooth reference functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(s\in\partial\omega(x)\), define
\[
D_\omega^{s}(y,x):=\omega(y)-\omega(x)-\langle s,y-x\rangle.
\]
The function \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex relative to \(\omega\) on \(C\), with \(\mu>0\), if for every \(x,y\in C\), every \(v\in\partial f(x)\), and every selected \(s\in\partial\omega(x)\),
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\mu D_\omega^{s}(y,x).
\]
If \(\omega(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), this reduces to ordinary strong convexity with modulus \(\mu\). In a DC analysis, the condition is imposed on the convex component or surrogate specified by the decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative strong convexity replaces squared Euclidean distance in the strong-convexity inequality by a Bregman divergence generated by a convex reference function.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex, and \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\omega:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex.
\(f\) and \(\omega\) are subdifferentiable at every base point under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\mu D_\omega^{s}(y,x)\) for all admissible \(x,y,v,s\).

notation.meaning: generalized Bregman divergence generated by a selected subgradient

children.title: Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective-growth settings used to control local convergence behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Convergence Without Distance Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of objective-to-distance conversion when no global growth regime holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[f(x)=\frac{x^2}{1+x^4}\quad(x\in\mathbb R).\] Then \(f_*=0\) and \(X_*=\{0\}\), but for \(x_k=k\), \[f(x_k)=\frac{k^2}{1+k^4}\to0=f_*,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x_k,X_*)=k\to\infty.\] Hence objective convergence alone does not imply convergence in distance to the minimizer set, and this function cannot satisfy a global order-\(p\) growth inequality with \(p\ge1\) and positive modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence can approach the optimal value while escaping from the minimizer set when global growth fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_k)\to f_*\quad\text{while}\quad\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X_*)\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Convergence Without Distance Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conversion of Objective Gaps to Distance Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct rate conversion supplied by an order-p growth regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \[f(x)-f_*\ge\frac{\alpha}{p}\operatorname{dist}(x,X_*)^p\] on \(U\), then every \(x\in U\) satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X_*)\le\left(\frac{p}{\alpha}(f(x)-f_*)\right)^{1/p}.\] Consequently, if \(x^k\in U\) and \(f(x^k)-f_*=O(\rho^k)\) for \(0<\rho<1\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(x^k,X_*)=O(\rho^{k/p})\); if the objective gap is \(O(k^{-r})\), then the distance is \(O(k^{-r/p})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order-p growth converts objective-gap rates into distance-to-solution rates by taking a p-th root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,X_*)\le\left(\frac{p}{\alpha}(f(x)-f_*)\right)^{1/p}.
knowledge_statements.title: Conversion of Objective Gaps to Distance Rates

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and has a nonempty minimizer set \(X_*:=\operatorname{argmin}f\).
\(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) is the region on which growth is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f_*\ge (\alpha/p)\operatorname{dist}(x,X_*)^p\) for every \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder growth condition; quadratic growth is the case \(p=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The objective \(f\) satisfies an order-\(p\) growth regime with modulus \(\alpha>0\) on \(U\), where \(p\ge1\), when
\[
f(x)-f_*\ge \frac{\alpha}{p}\operatorname{dist}^{p}(x,X_*)
\quad\text{for all }x\in U,
\]
with \(f_*:=\min f\) and \(X_*:=\operatorname{argmin}f\). The regime is quadratic growth when \(p=2\). In DC convergence analysis, \(U\) may be restricted to a sublevel set containing the DCA iterates; no convexity of the pointwise DC objective is part of the definition. The condition converts objective convergence into convergence in distance to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-p growth regime lower-bounds objective suboptimality by a positive multiple of the p-th power of distance to the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Growth Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-p growth condition is precise and fits the leaf, but its normalization and the DC/DCA-specific sublevel-set application have no inspectable citation.

children.title: Regime Implication Structure
children.top_down_role: Implications and separations among relative convexity and growth conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Growth Does Not Imply Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex Euclidean separation of the strong-convexity and quadratic-growth regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). Then \(X_*=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\) and \[f(x)-f_*=\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X_*).\] Thus global quadratic growth holds, but \(f\) is not strongly convex because it is constant along every line \(\{x_1\}\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared distance to a non-singleton subspace has global quadratic growth but is not strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f_*=\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X_*)\), while \(f\) is not strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth Does Not Imply Strong Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convex Regime Implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globally valid convex baseline; localized versions require the comparison minimizer and all required inequalities to share the stated region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, closed, convex, attain \(f_*\), and set \(X_*:=\operatorname{argmin}f\) and \(r(x):=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\). If \(f\) is globally \(\alpha\)-strongly convex, then \[f(x)-f_*\geq \frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X_*),\qquad f(x)-f_*\leq\frac{r(x)^2}{2\alpha}.\] More generally, global quadratic growth \[f(x)-f_*\geq\frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X_*)\] implies \[f(x)-f_*\leq\frac{2}{\alpha}r(x)^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global convex strong convexity implies quadratic growth and a residual PL bound; convex quadratic growth alone still implies a weaker residual bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and attains its minimum.
The asserted strong-convexity or quadratic-growth inequality holds globally with \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\)-strong convexity implies quadratic growth and \(f-f_*\le r^2/(2\alpha)\); quadratic growth implies \(f-f_*\le 2r^2/\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.title: Global Convex Regime Implications

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, attains \(f_*\), and \(X_*:=\operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\).
All asserted inequalities hold on the same convex region \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong convexity implies quadratic growth and a PL inequality; quadratic growth implies a PL inequality with a weaker constant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex baseline implication chain; DC extensions require decomposition-specific hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r(x):=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\). If \(f\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly convex on \(U\), then
\[
f(x)-f_*\ge \frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}^{2}(x,X_*)
\quad\text{and}\quad
f(x)-f_*\le \frac{r(x)^2}{2\alpha}.
\]
If instead only quadratic growth
\[
f(x)-f_*\ge \frac{\alpha}{2}\operatorname{dist}^{2}(x,X_*)
\]
is assumed, convexity and the subgradient inequality imply
\[
f(x)-f_*\le \frac{2}{\alpha}r(x)^2.
\]
Thus relative or ordinary strong convexity supplies growth, and growth supplies a PL-type residual bound, although reverse implications need not hold without additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex objectives, strong convexity yields quadratic growth and PL; quadratic growth also yields PL, generally with a weaker constant. Reverse implications require extra assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Regime Implication Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication structure is plausible, but the constants and localized formulation require a source. The assumptions also do not ensure that projections or comparison segments needed for the stated inequalities remain in the common region U.

children.title: Local Versus Global Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distinction between neighborhood-based conditions and globally valid conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Quadratic Growth Need Not Globalize
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation between local and global growth regimes around the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[f(x)=\frac{x^2}{1+x^2},\qquad S=\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{0\}.\] For \(|x|\le1\), \[f(x)\ge\frac12x^2=\frac12\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2,\] so local quadratic growth holds. However, for every \(\mu>0\), the global inequality \(f(x)\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) fails for sufficiently large \(|x|\), because \[\frac{f(x)}{x^2}=\frac1{1+x^2}\to0.\] Moreover, \(f\) is finite-valued DC on \(\mathbb R\), since it is twice continuously differentiable with second derivative bounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded smooth DC objective can have quadratic growth near its unique minimizer while admitting no positive global quadratic-growth constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\ge\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) for \(|x|\le1\), but no \(\mu>0\) gives \(f(x)\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Quadratic Growth Need Not Globalize

assumptions_latex: \(P(x)\) is a growth, error-bound, or PL predicate defined for points in \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
\(S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) is the reference solution or critical set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global validity requires \(P(x)\) on all of \(\operatorname{dom}f\); local validity requires it only where \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\rho\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization convention for growth-regularity assumptions used in DCA convergence statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A regularity regime \(P\) is global when \(P(x)\) holds for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). It is local around a nonempty reference set \(S\) when there exists \(\rho>0\) such that
\[
P(x)\quad\text{holds whenever}\quad x\in\operatorname{dom}f
\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\rho.
\]
A sublevel-local regime additionally restricts these points by \(f(x)\le c\) for a specified \(c\). A local regime can support an eventual DCA rate only after the iterates are shown to enter and remain in its neighborhood. A global regime requires no such entry argument but is strictly stronger than its localized counterpart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is global if it holds throughout the domain and local if it holds only near a specified solution or critical set.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Versus Global Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local/global definitions fit the leaf, but the eventual-DCA-rate assertion needs support. Calling the global regime strictly stronger is overstated without qualifications; global validity implies local validity, but strict separation is problem-dependent.

children.title: Polyhedral DCA Convergence
children.top_down_role: Finite convergence and identification phenomena are isolated from general asymptotic theory.

assumptions_latex: Exactly one of \(g\) and \(h\) is assumed polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition belongs to a one-component polyhedral regime, without thereby implying finite DCA termination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural regime only; convergence consequences depend on which component is polyhedral and on the DCA selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The DC decomposition \(f=g-h\) is in a one-component polyhedral regime when either \(g\) or \(h\), but not necessarily both, is polyhedral convex. Equivalently, for one component \(\varphi\in\{g,h\}\), the epigraph
\[
\operatorname{epi}\varphi:=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:t\ge\varphi(x)\}
\]
is a polyhedron. The other component may be nonpolyhedral. This assumption gives finitely many faces or subgradient cells only for the polyhedral component. Consequently, it does not by itself make the DCA update map finite-valued, nor does it alone guarantee identification or finite termination; those conclusions require additional uniqueness, nondegeneracy, or descent hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-component polyhedral regime means that one convex DC component has a polyhedral epigraph, while the other component may remain nonpolyhedral.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Component Polyhedral Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assumptions require exactly one component to be polyhedral, whereas the statement says one component is polyhedral but not necessarily only one. A source is needed to determine whether this regime excludes or includes fully polyhedral decompositions and to support the negative convergence claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Subdifferential Stratification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite primal-dual cell structure induced by both polyhedral convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g\) and \(h\) are proper closed polyhedral convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), then \(\operatorname{gph}\partial g\) and \(\operatorname{gph}\partial h\) are finite unions of polyhedral convex sets. Each effective domain admits a finite polyhedral stratification such that, on the relative interior of every stratum, the active affine indices, the active domain face, and the corresponding polyhedral subdifferential value are constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each polyhedral DC component has a finite stratification on whose relative-interior cells its active affine pieces, domain face, and polyhedral subdifferential are fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are proper closed polyhedral convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}\partial g\text{ and }\operatorname{gph}\partial h\text{ are finite unions of polyhedral convex sets}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Subdifferential Stratification

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both \(\operatorname{epi}g\) and \(\operatorname{epi}h\) are polyhedra, so each component has a finite max-affine representation on its domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real polyhedral DC representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A DC decomposition is fully polyhedral when both \(g\) and \(h\) are polyhedral convex. In finite dimensions, this is equivalent to the existence of polyhedral domains \(P_g,P_h\), finite sets \(I,J\), and affine coefficients such that
\[
g(x)=\max_{i\in I}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}+\delta_{P_g}(x),
\qquad
h(x)=\max_{j\in J}\{\langle c_j,x\rangle+d_j\}+\delta_{P_h}(x).
\]
Hence the decomposition has finitely many primal faces and finitely many affine subgradient cells. This finite combinatorial structure is the basis for identification and termination results, but finite termination still requires an update rule that cannot move indefinitely within an identified face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully polyhedral DC decomposition represents both convex components as finite maxima of affine functions over polyhedral domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Fully Polyhedral DC Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional max-affine representation fits the fully polyhedral leaf, but no source with a specific locator supports the equivalence or the identification/termination qualification.

children.title: Finite-Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral settings supporting termination after finitely many DCA iterations.

assumptions_latex: The DCA state set \(\mathcal S\) reachable from the initial point is finite.
The deterministic update map \(T:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S\) strictly decreases \(f\) whenever \(T(s)\ne s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some \(K<|\mathcal S|\) satisfies \(T(s^K)=s^K\), so DCA terminates after finitely many strict updates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-state termination criterion for a deterministic polyhedral DCA realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s^{k+1}=T(s^k)\) be a deterministic DCA realization on a finite reachable state set \(\mathcal S\). Assume that each state determines its primal iterate and that
\[
T(s)\ne s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(T(s))<f(s).
\]
Then no nonfixed state can be revisited. Therefore there exists an index \(K<|\mathcal S|\) such that
\[
T(s^K)=s^K.
\]
The associated primal iterate is stationary for the selected DCA update rule, and the algorithm terminates after at most \(|\mathcal S|-1\) strict transitions. Polyhedrality supports this theorem only when it actually reduces the chosen state description to finitely many reachable states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic DCA terminates finitely when it has finitely many reachable states and every nonfixed update strictly decreases the objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Termination Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-state descent argument is coherent and theorem is the correct content kind, but the DCA state-to-objective mapping and the claim that a fixed state yields stationarity for the selected DCA rule require a cited formalization.

children.title: Active-Structure Identification
children.top_down_role: Eventual stabilization of active pieces, faces, or related structural data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eventual Exclusion of Limit-Inactive Pieces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The unconditional active-set information supplied by convergence for a finite max-affine component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi(x)=\max_{i\in I}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}\), where \(I\) is finite, and let \(x^k\to\bar x\). Then every index inactive at \(\bar x\) is inactive for all sufficiently large \(k\); equivalently, \[\limsup_{k\to\infty} I(x^k)\subseteq I(\bar x).\] Exact eventual equality \(I(x^k)=I(\bar x)\) requires an additional identification condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence eventually eliminates every affine piece inactive at the limit, although it does not by itself force the remaining active set to stabilize exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \limsup_{k\to\infty}I(x^k)\subseteq I(\bar x).

notation.meaning: indices attaining the finite affine maximum at x
indices occurring infinitely often along the active sets

knowledge_statements.title: Eventual Exclusion of Limit-Inactive Pieces
Active-Structure Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification of polyhedral faces or affine pieces along DCA iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a polyhedral component
\[
\varphi(x)=\max_{i\in I}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}+\delta_P(x),
\]
define its active set by
\[
I(x):=\{i\in I:\varphi(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}
\]
whenever \(x\in P\). A DCA sequence identifies an active structure if there exist \(K\) and a fixed active set \(I_*\), face \(F_*\), or subgradient cell \(Q_*\) such that for every \(k\ge K\), respectively \(I(x^k)=I_*\), \(x^k\in\operatorname{ri}F_*\), or \(y^k\in\operatorname{ri}Q_*\). Identification means stabilization of combinatorial structure; it does not require the numerical iterates themselves to become constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active-structure identification occurs when the affine pieces, polyhedral face, or subgradient cell selected by DCA eventually stops changing.
assumptions_latex: A polyhedral convex component has a finite affine representation indexed by \(I\).
The DCA iterates \(x^k\) and selected subgradients \(y^k\) are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identification occurs when the active primal and dual structures are constant for all sufficiently large \(k\).

notation.meaning: active affine pieces at a point

children.title: Identification-to-Termination Relations
children.top_down_role: Circumstances linking stabilized active structure to finite termination.

assumptions_latex: After some index \(K\), all DCA states lie in one identified polyhedral structure \(\mathcal F_*\).
The update restricted to \(\mathcal F_*\) is deterministic, has finite image, and strictly decreases \(f\) at every nonfixed state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identified DCA sequence reaches a fixed point after finitely many additional updates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient bridge from finite active-set identification to finite DCA termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that from iteration \(K\) onward, the DCA state belongs to an identified polyhedral structure \(\mathcal F_*\). Let \(T_*\) denote the update restricted to that structure. If \(T_*\) is deterministic, its reachable image is finite, and
\[
T_*(s)\ne s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(T_*(s))<f(s),
\]
then the sequence reaches a fixed point of \(T_*\) after finitely many iterations beyond \(K\). Identification alone is insufficient: when the restricted subproblem has multiple minimizers or a continuum of admissible states, the iterates may keep moving inside \(\mathcal F_*\) without changing active structure. Thus termination follows from identification only together with finite-state or uniqueness and strict-descent conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identification yields finite termination only when the restricted update has finitely many states, or suitable uniqueness, and strictly decreases at every nonfixed state.
knowledge_statements.title: Identification-to-Termination Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-image strict-descent implication is coherent and fits the leaf, but no source supports its DCA interpretation. The final reference to uniqueness is also not formulated as a sufficient hypothesis in the formal statement.

children.title: Degenerate Polyhedral Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy or ambiguity that prevents identification or termination conclusions.

assumptions_latex: DCA permits arbitrary selections from convex subdifferentials and subproblem minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polyhedrality and active-face stability do not guarantee finite termination when the DCA subproblem is degenerate and nonunique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete degeneracy showing that full polyhedrality does not itself force termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x)=h(x)=|x|\), so \(f(x)=0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\). Start with \(x^0>0\) and choose \(y^k=1\in\partial h(x^k)\). The DCA subproblem is
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}\{|x|-x\}=[0,+\infty).
\]
Choosing, for example, \(x^{k+1}=1/(k+2)\) produces infinitely many distinct iterates, all with the same objective value and the same positive affine piece active. Both components are polyhedral and the active structure is already identified, yet the sequence does not terminate. The failure is caused by degeneracy and nonuniqueness of the convex subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For g=h=absolute value, DCA may select infinitely many distinct positive minimizers despite full polyhedrality and an already stable active piece.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Polyhedral Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit selection sequence is mathematically consistent and the counterexample kind fits this failure-boundary leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable evidence for its use as a DCA boundary example.

children.title: DCA Rate-Certificate Complexity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Nonasymptotic families are indexed by the certificate actually measured and the smoothness or inexactness regime.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: On the Rate of Convergence of the Difference-of-Convex Algorithm
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sections on smooth decompositions, nonsmooth stopping criteria, and PL rates
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: On the Rate of Convergence of the Difference-of-Convex Algorithm

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth-Decomposition Stationarity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact smooth DCA with strong convexity of the minimized component and Lipschitz gradient of the linearized component on a common region containing the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=g-h\). On a convex set containing every iterate and update segment, suppose \(g\) is differentiable and \(\sigma\)-strongly convex, \(h\) is differentiable, and \(\nabla h\) is \(L_h\)-Lipschitz. Assume the exact DCA subproblem has a solution satisfying
\[\nabla g(x^{k+1})=\nabla h(x^k).
\]
For \(r(x):=\nabla g(x)-\nabla h(x)\), if \(f(x^k)\ge f_*>-\infty\), then
\[\min_{1\le j\le K}\|r(x^j)\|^2\le\frac{2L_h^2\bigl(f(x^0)-f_*\bigr)}{\sigma K}.
\]
Thus \(\|r(x^j)\|\le\varepsilon\) occurs within \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) exact DCA steps. The conclusion requires both quadratic descent and Lipschitz conversion of the step into the stated gradient residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strong-convexity descent and Lipschitz control of the linearized component's gradient, exact smooth DCA reaches an epsilon gradient-difference residual in order epsilon-to-the-minus-two steps.
assumptions_latex: A common convex region containing the iterates and update segments supports the stated differentiability, strong-convexity, and Lipschitz assumptions.
Each exact DCA subproblem attains a point satisfying \(\nabla g(x^{k+1})=\nabla h(x^k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{1\le j\le K}\|\nabla g(x^j)-\nabla h(x^j)\|^2\le 2L_h^2(f(x^0)-f_*)/(\sigma K).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the gradient of h

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-Decomposition Stationarity Complexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional Nonsmooth-Decomposition Residual Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate rate for exact DCA under explicit quadratic descent and residual-to-step control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=g-h\), with proper closed convex \(g,h\). Suppose exact DCA selects \(y^k\in\partial h(x^k)\) and \(x^{k+1}\) with \(y^k\in\partial g(x^{k+1})\). Define
\[r_{k+1}:=\operatorname{dist}(y^k,\partial h(x^{k+1})).\]
If, for constants \(a,b>0\),
\[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,\qquad r_{k+1}\le b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|,
\]
and \(F(x^k)\ge F_{\inf}>-\infty\), then
\[\min_{0\le k<K}r_{k+1}\le b\sqrt{\frac{F(x^0)-F_{\inf}}{aK}}.
\]
Moreover, \(r_{k+1}=0\) implies \(\partial g(x^{k+1})\cap\partial h(x^{k+1})\ne\varnothing\). The residual and its bound depend on the chosen DC decomposition and selected subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic descent plus residual-to-step control yields an order K-to-the-minus-one-half best-iterate decomposition residual.
assumptions_latex: The displayed exact DCA inclusions hold.
The displayed descent and residual-to-step inequalities hold with \(a,b>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{0\le k<K}r_{k+1}\le b\sqrt{(F(x^0)-F_{\inf})/(aK)}.

notation.meaning: finite lower bound along the iterates

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Nonsmooth-Decomposition Residual Complexity
Nonsmooth-Decomposition Residual Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional best-iterate residual rate for exact DCA with a nonsmooth DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=g-h\), where \(g,h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper closed convex functions. Suppose exact DCA produces \(y^k\in\partial h(x^k)\) and \(x^{k+1}\) satisfying \(y^k\in\partial g(x^{k+1})\). Define \(r_{k+1}=\operatorname{dist}(y^k,\partial h(x^{k+1}))\). If \(F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert^2\), \(r_{k+1}\le b\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\), and \(F\ge F_{\inf}>-\infty\), then
\[\min_{0\le k<K}r_{k+1}\le b\sqrt{\frac{F(x^0)-F_{\inf}}{aK}}.\]
Thus an iterate with residual at most \(\varepsilon\) occurs within \(K=O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) DCA steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under quadratic descent and a residual-to-step bound, exact nonsmooth DCA attains a decomposition residual at most epsilon in order epsilon-to-the-minus-two iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are proper closed convex functions.
\(F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert^2\) and \(r_{k+1}\le b\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\), with \(a,b>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le k<K}r_{k+1}\le b\sqrt{(F(x^0)-F_{\inf})/(aK)}\).

notation.meaning: DC objective and its selected convex decomposition
finite lower bound for the objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional best-iterate bound is mathematically consistent and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but no cited source supports this DCA residual definition or the assumed residual-to-step estimate.

children.title: Step-Norm Certificates
children.top_down_role: Complexity certificates based on the magnitude of successive iterate displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square Summability Does Not Imply Finite Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-level boundary separating vanishing square-summable steps from summable trajectory length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonnegative step sequence \(s_k=1/(k+1)\) satisfies \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}s_k^2<\infty\) and \(s_k\to0\), while \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}s_k=+\infty\). Therefore the square-summability conclusion furnished by quadratic descent cannot alone establish finite trajectory length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Harmonic-size steps vanish and are square summable but have infinite total length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_k s_k^2<\infty\quad\text{but}\quad\sum_k s_k=+\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Square Summability Does Not Imply Finite Length

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square Summability of DCA Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic step property under quadratic sufficient decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_k:=\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\). If \[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a s_k^2\] for some \(a>0\) and \(F(x^k)\ge F_{\inf}>-\infty\), then \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}s_k^2\le\frac{F(x^0)-F_{\inf}}{a}<\infty,\qquad s_k\to0.\] Square summability alone does not imply finite trajectory length \(\sum_k s_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic descent makes squared step norms summable and forces individual steps to vanish, but does not by itself give finite length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert^2<\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\to0.

notation.meaning: norm of the kth DCA step

knowledge_statements.title: Square Summability of DCA Steps
Step-Norm Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directly computable finite-iteration certificate derived from consecutive DCA iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For DCA iterates \((x^k)\), define the step certificate \(s_k=\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\). If the accepted update satisfies
\[F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a s_k^2\]
for some \(a>0\), then observing \(s_k\le\varepsilon\) certifies both an \(\varepsilon\)-small update and the guaranteed decrease bound \(F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a s_k^2\). Moreover, if \(F\ge F_{\inf}\), then among the first \(K\) steps,
\[\min_{0\le k<K}s_k\le\sqrt{\frac{F(x^0)-F_{\inf}}{aK}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The norm of a DCA update is computable from two iterates and, under quadratic descent, supplies a best-iterate certificate decreasing as one over square root of the iteration count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le k<K}s_k\le\sqrt{(F(x^0)-F_{\inf})/(aK)}\).

notation.meaning: norm of the kth DCA step

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate and telescoping bound are correct under the stated quadratic-descent assumption, and certificate is the appropriate kind. A source is required for this assumption in the intended DCA setting.

children.title: Objective-Decrease Certificates
children.top_down_role: Complexity certificates based on achieved objective reduction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-Boundedness Boundary for Vanishing Decreases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of summability and vanishing when a monotone objective sequence has no finite lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scalar sequence \(F_k=-k\) is monotone decreasing and has \(d_k:=F_k-F_{k+1}=1\) for every \(k\). Thus monotonicity without a finite lower bound does not imply summability or vanishing of objective decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone sequence can decrease by a fixed positive amount forever when it is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_k=1\ \text{for all }k,\quad \sum_k d_k=+\infty,\quad d_k\not\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Boundedness Boundary for Vanishing Decreases

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Summability and Vanishing of Objective Decreases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic consequence of a lower-bounded monotone objective sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F(x^{k+1})\le F(x^k)\), \(F(x^k)\ge F_{\inf}>-\infty\), and \(d_k:=F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\), then \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d_k\le F(x^0)-F_{\inf}<\infty.\] Consequently, \(d_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative decreases of a lower-bounded monotone objective sequence are summable and therefore vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d_k<\infty\quad\text{and}\quad d_k\to0.

notation.meaning: finite lower bound along the trajectory

knowledge_statements.title: Summability and Vanishing of Objective Decreases
Objective-Decrease Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate based on the observed decrease of a monotone DCA objective sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x^{k+1})\le F(x^k)\) and define the objective-decrease certificate \(d_k=F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge0\). If \(F\ge F_{\inf}>-\infty\), telescoping gives
\[\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}d_k=F(x^0)-F(x^K)\le F(x^0)-F_{\inf},\]
and hence
\[\min_{0\le k<K}d_k\le\frac{F(x^0)-F_{\inf}}{K}.\]
Thus \(d_k\) is a verifiable progress certificate, and a decrease no larger than \(\varepsilon\) must occur within \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-bounded monotone DCA sequence, the smallest observed objective decrease among the first K steps is at most the initial objective gap divided by K.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le k<K}d_k\le(F(x^0)-F_{\inf})/K\).

notation.meaning: objective decrease across the kth update
finite lower bound for the objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The telescoping calculation and best-iterate decrease bound are correct, and the selected kind fits. No source establishes the monotone lower-bounded DCA setting invoked by the record.

children.title: Certificate Comparability
children.top_down_role: Regimes permitting translation between step-based and decrease-based measures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of One-Sided Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar families showing that neither one-sided comparison supplies the reverse vanishing implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(s_k=1/(k+1)\) and \(d_k=1\), the lower comparison \(d_k\ge s_k^2\) holds and \(s_k\to0\), but \(d_k\not\to0\). For \(s_k=1\) and \(d_k=0\), the upper comparison \(d_k\le s_k^2\) holds and \(d_k\to0\), but \(s_k\not\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower comparison alone does not turn vanishing steps into vanishing decreases, and an upper comparison alone does not turn vanishing decreases into vanishing steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_k\ge a s_k^2\not\Rightarrow(s_k\to0\Rightarrow d_k\to0),\qquad d_k\le b s_k^2\not\Rightarrow(d_k\to0\Rightarrow s_k\to0).

notation.meaning: abstract nonnegative step and decrease certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of One-Sided Comparability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Certificate Translations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold implications supplied by each direction of a quadratic step–decrease comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_k,d_k\ge0\). If \(d_k\ge a s_k^2\) for some \(a>0\), then \(d_k\le\varepsilon\) implies \(s_k\le\sqrt{\varepsilon/a}\). If \(d_k\le b s_k^2\) for some \(b<\infty\), then \(s_k\le\varepsilon\) implies \(d_k\le b\varepsilon^2\). Thus each one-sided comparison translates thresholds in one direction; the two comparisons together imply equivalence of vanishing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower quadratic comparison translates small decrease into a small step, while an upper comparison translates a small step into small decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(d_k\ge a s_k^2\) with \(a>0\) for the first implication.
\(d_k\le b s_k^2\) with \(b<\infty\) for the second implication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_k\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow s_k\le\sqrt{\varepsilon/a},\qquad s_k\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow d_k\le b\varepsilon^2.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Certificate Translations
Certificate Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided comparison between step-norm and objective-decrease certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(s_k=\lVert x^{k+1}-x^k\rVert\) and \(d_k=F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\), suppose constants \(0<a\le b<\infty\) satisfy
\[a s_k^2\le d_k\le b s_k^2\]
for every accepted DCA step. Then
\[\sqrt{d_k/b}\le s_k\le\sqrt{d_k/a}.\]
Consequently, \(s_k\to0\) if and only if \(d_k\to0\), and thresholds for either certificate translate explicitly into thresholds for the other. Without the upper comparison, small objective decrease need not certify a small step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When objective decrease is bounded above and below by constant multiples of squared step norm, the two certificates vanish together and their stopping thresholds are interchangeable.
assumptions_latex: \(a s_k^2\le d_k\le b s_k^2\) for constants \(0<a\le b<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt{d_k/b}\le s_k\le\sqrt{d_k/a}\), and \(s_k\to0\Longleftrightarrow d_k\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic comparison and equivalence of vanishing certificates follow from the stated two-sided inequality. The property kind fits, but the DCA-specific upper comparison is substantial and unsupported.

children.title: Vanishing-Certificate Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits of interpreting small steps or small decreases as strong stationarity evidence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Step and Decrease at a Nonminimum DC-Critical Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that vanishing progress certificates do not certify local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=g(x)-h(x)\) on \(\mathbb R\), where \(g(x)=x^4\) and \(h(x)=x^2\). At \(x^0=0\), choose \(y^0=0\in\partial h(0)\). The DCA subproblem \[x^1\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}\{g(x)-y^0x\}\] has the unique solution \(x^1=0\); repeating this choice gives \(x^k=0\), so every step norm and objective decrease is zero.
