knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_j\to u\) and \(v_j\to v\) imply \(u\in\partial g(x)\) and \(v\in\partial h(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind fits the representation-consistency leaf. The graphical outer-consistency definition is plausible, but the claimed sufficient regime based on local uniform convergence needs an authoritative source specifying the neighborhood, finiteness, and subgradient convergence assumptions. No evidence is cited.

children.title: Sequential Convergence for Quasi-DC Descent
children.top_down_role: Whole-sequence results are organized by their distinct compactness, isolation, finite-length, and regularity mechanisms without importing DCA-specific KL claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Steps Without an Isolated Cluster Point Need Not Converge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for the isolated-cluster convergence mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a sequence in \([0,1]\) by alternately traversing from \(0\) to \(1\) and back, using \(N_m=2^m\) equal increments during traversal \(m\). Then \(|x^{k+1}-x^k|\to0\), the sequence is bounded, and its cluster set is \([0,1]\), but the sequence does not converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded sequence can have vanishing steps while repeatedly traversing a continuum of cluster points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Boundedness and \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\) do not imply convergence without an isolation mechanism.

notation.meaning: number of equal steps in traversal m

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Steps Without an Isolated Cluster Point Need Not Converge
Isolated-Cluster-Point Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-sequence convergence obtained from asymptotic regularity and an isolated cluster point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x^k)\) be a bounded sequence in \(\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\). Its cluster set \(\Omega\) is nonempty, compact, and connected. Consequently, if some \(\bar x\in\Omega\) is isolated relative to \(\Omega\), then \(\Omega=\{\bar x\}\) and
\[
x^k\to\bar x.
\]
Thus a quasi-DC descent sequence converges completely whenever its descent analysis gives asymptotic regularity and its cluster set contains an isolated point; if all cluster points are critical, the limit is critical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded asymptotically regular sequence converges when its cluster set contains an isolated point.
assumptions_latex: The cluster set contains a relatively isolated point \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\to\bar x\).

notation.meaning: set of cluster points of the iterate sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the sequential-convergence leaf. The bounded asymptotically regular sequence result is standard in finite dimensions, but this candidate supplies neither a citation nor a standard-field rationale for the connectedness of the cluster set and the isolated-point consequence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Length Tail Error Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-limit bound from the remaining path length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\|x^{j+1}-x^j\|<\infty\) and \(x^k\to\bar x\), then \[\|x^k-\bar x\|\le\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\|x^{j+1}-x^j\|.\] Therefore any computable upper bound on the remaining step-length tail certifies distance to the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The untraveled tail length bounds the current distance to the limit.
assumptions_latex: The iterate path has finite total length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x^k-\bar x\|\le\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\|x^{j+1}-x^j\|\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Length Tail Error Certificate
Finite-Length Quasi-DC Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential convergence from summability of quasi-DC step lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x^k)\subset\mathbb R^n\) satisfy the finite-length condition
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty.
\]
Then \((x^k)\) is Cauchy and converges to some \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\). If, additionally, the quasi-DC residuals tend to zero and the employed representations are subdifferentially consistent at \(\bar x\), then
\[
\partial g(\bar x)\cap\partial h(\bar x)\ne\varnothing.
\]
Hence finite length upgrades subsequential criticality to convergence of the entire sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable step lengths force the entire iterate sequence to converge; consistent vanishing residuals make its limit DC-critical.
assumptions_latex: The representations are subdifferentially consistent at the limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\to\bar x\) and \(\partial g(\bar x)\cap\partial h(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the finite-length leaf, and finite length alone correctly implies convergence in R^n. However, the additional criticality conclusion invokes unspecified quasi-DC residuals and an informal consistency condition, so its exact hypotheses cannot be verified without a source and a precise residual definition.

children.title: Error-Bound Quasi-DC Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sequential convergence settings organized by quasi-DC error bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power-KL Convergence-Rate Trichotomy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard rate consequences once sufficient decrease, relative error, attentive convergence, and the power-form KL inequality all hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the standard sufficient-decrease and limiting-subdifferential relative-error estimates, attentive convergence to \(x^*\), and a KL inequality with \(\varphi(s)=cs^{1-\theta}\), \(c>0\), \(\theta\in[0,1)\), throughout the eventual iterate neighborhood. Then \(\theta=0\) yields finite termination; \(0<\theta\le\tfrac12\) yields at least geometric convergence; and \(\tfrac12<\theta<1\) yields \[F(x^k)-F_* =O\!\left(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)}\right),\qquad \|x^k-x^*\|=O\!\left(k^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-type KL bound gives finite, geometric, or polynomial convergence according to its exponent.
assumptions_latex: Sufficient decrease and a limiting-subdifferential relative-error estimate hold.
The iterates converge attentively to \(x^*\) and eventually remain in a uniform KL neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite, geometric, or polynomial rate stated for the corresponding exponent range holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-KL Convergence-Rate Trichotomy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attentive Cluster-Value Requirement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-continuity condition needed to apply a KL error bound at cluster points of a descent sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F(x^k)\downarrow F_*\) and \(x^{k_j}\to\bar x\), the standard cluster-set KL argument requires \(F(x^{k_j})\to F(\bar x)=F_*\). Lower semicontinuity alone yields only \(F(\bar x)\le F_*\) and does not provide the needed equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a KL inequality at a cluster point requires objective-value convergence to that point; lower semicontinuity alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The additional equality \(F(x^{k_j})\to F(\bar x)=F_*\) is required by the standard cluster-set KL argument.

notation.meaning: limiting objective value along the sequence

knowledge_statements.title: Attentive Cluster-Value Requirement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz Error-Bound Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local desingularized criticality inequality defining the regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\), and \(F_*=F(\bar x)\). The KL property holds at \(\bar x\) if there are a neighborhood \(U\), \(\eta>0\), and a continuous concave \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb R_+\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\varphi\in C^1(0,\eta)\), and \(\varphi'>0\), such that \[\varphi'(F(x)-F_*)\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\ge1\] whenever \(x\in U\) and \(F_*<F(x)<F_*+\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KL regime bounds a desingularized objective slope away from zero near a reference value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed KL inequality holds on a punctured objective neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz Error-Bound Regime
Error-Bound Quasi-DC Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite length under sufficient decrease, relative error, and a desingularizing error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let a bounded quasi-DC sequence satisfy
\[
F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,
\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x^{k+1}))\le b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|
\]
for \(a,b>0\). Suppose that near its compact cluster set, for \(F_*<F(x)<F_*+\eta\), a concave \(C^1\) function \(\varphi\) with \(\varphi'>0\) satisfies
\[
\varphi'(F(x)-F_*)\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\ge1.
\]
Then \(\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty\), so \(x^k\) converges to a critical point of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KL-type error bound combined with sufficient decrease and relative error yields finite length and convergence to a critical point.
assumptions_latex: The sequence is bounded and satisfies sufficient decrease.
A relative-error estimate holds for the limiting subdifferential.
The displayed uniform desingularizing error bound holds near the cluster set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty\) and \(x^k\to\bar x\) with \(0\in\partial F(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: common objective value on the cluster set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the error-bound regime leaf, but no source supports this KL-type convergence theorem. The formulation does not explicitly ensure the required value-continuity/attentive convergence at cluster points, nor does it define F_* in the statement before using it as the common cluster-set value; these details affect the critical-limit conclusion.

children.title: Regular Quasi-DC Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sequential convergence settings organized by regularity properties.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Subregularity Does Not Imply Strong Metric Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology boundary between a residual error bound and local single-valued invertibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(x)=\{x,-x\}\). Then \(\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x))=|x|\), so \(|x|\le\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x))\) and \(M\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((0,0)\). For every small \(y\ne0\), however, \(M^{-1}(y)=\{y,-y\}\), so the localized inverse is not single-valued. Thus strong metric subregularity is not strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual bound can isolate a zero without making the inverse mapping locally single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong metric subregularity does not imply strong metric regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Subregularity Does Not Imply Strong Metric Regularity
Regular Quasi-DC Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong metric subregularity of the decomposition-criticality mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed representation \(f=g-h\), define the criticality mapping
\[
M(x):=\partial g(x)-\partial h(x).
\]
A critical point \(\bar x\) is strongly regular in the quasi-DC sense if \(0\in M(\bar x)\) and there exist \(\kappa,r>0\) such that
\[
\|x-\bar x\|\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x))
\quad\text{whenever }\|x-\bar x\|<r.
\]
This error bound makes \(\bar x\) the unique zero of \(M\) in that neighborhood and converts a vanishing criticality residual into a local distance estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong regularity bounds distance to a critical point by the decomposition-criticality residual and locally isolates that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-\bar x\|\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x))\) locally, and \(M^{-1}(0)\cap B_r(\bar x)=\{\bar x\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind fits the regular-regime leaf. The displayed inequality is strong metric subregularity of M at (bar x,0), and it does imply local isolation of the zero. Calling this property strong regularity is potentially misleading, and no source establishes the intended quasi-DC terminology or mapping convention.

children.title: Regime Overlap
children.top_down_role: Shared cases and implication relations between the two regime families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Isolation, Residual Error Bounds, and KL Bounds Are Distinct
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implication boundary among isolated-zero, strong-subregularity, and KL regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a criticality mapping \(M\), strong metric subregularity at \((\bar x,0)\), \[\|x-\bar x\|\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,M(x)),\] implies that \(\bar x\) is an isolated zero of \(M\). The converse fails: \(M(x)=x^2\) has isolated zero \(0\), but \(|x|\le\kappa|x|^2\) cannot hold near zero. Neither property alone supplies a KL inequality for an objective or the descent and relative-error estimates needed for finite length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear residual error bound implies isolation, but isolation does not imply that bound, and neither alone supplies the KL descent mechanism.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is considered locally at a zero \((\bar x,0)\).
Any KL assertion concerns a separately specified objective and subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{strong metric subregularity}\Rightarrow\text{isolated zero}\), while the converse and any automatic KL implication fail in general.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolation, Residual Error Bounds, and KL Bounds Are Distinct
Regime Overlap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interaction of error-bound, finite-length, and isolated-critical-point regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a bounded quasi-DC sequence satisfies the sufficient-decrease and relative-error inequalities of the error-bound regime, and a uniform desingularizing inequality holds near its cluster set. If the limiting criticality mapping \(M\) is strongly metrically subregular at a cluster point \((\bar x,0)\), then the error-bound argument gives
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty,
\]
while subregularity makes \(\bar x\) locally isolated among zeros of \(M\). Consequently the finite-length, error-bound, and isolated-critical-point regimes agree on the conclusion \(x^k\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an error-bound descent regime also has strong subregularity, finite length and isolation support the same full-sequence convergence conclusion.
assumptions_latex: The error-bound regime hypotheses hold near the cluster set.
\(M\) is strongly metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\).
\(\bar x\) is a cluster point of the sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty\) and \(x^k\to\bar x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind is suitable for a regime-overlap leaf. Its conclusion depends on the unsourced KL/error-bound theorem and on a precise relationship between zeros of M and all cluster points. With no citation, the combined hypotheses and conclusion cannot be reliably fixed.

children.title: Failure Outside Regularity
children.top_down_role: Sequential-convergence limitations when neither regime supplies adequate control.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Nonconvergence with Square-Summable Increments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete sequential counterexample with constant objective and zero criticality residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\equiv0\) on \(\mathbb R\) and \(x^k=\sin(\log(k+1))\). Then every point is critical, \(F(x^k)\) is constant, and \(|x^{k+1}-x^k|=O(1/k)\), so \(\sum_k|x^{k+1}-x^k|^2<\infty\). Nevertheless \((x^k)\) does not converge and its cluster set is \([-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded critical sequence can have square-summable increments and constant objective while oscillating over an entire interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual is zero and the increments are square summable, but the sequence does not converge.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Nonconvergence with Square-Summable Increments

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square-Summable Steps Do Not Imply Finite Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical-series boundary separating quadratic descent control from a Cauchy guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The implication \(\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2<\infty\Rightarrow\sum_k\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|<\infty\) is false. Thus a lower-bounded objective and an estimate \(F(x^k)-F(x^{k+1})\ge a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2\) may imply square summability and vanishing increments without proving that the iterates are Cauchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic sufficient decrease controls squared step lengths, which is weaker than finite length.
assumptions_latex: Only a quadratic sufficient-decrease estimate and a lower objective bound are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Square summability and vanishing increments need not imply finite length or convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Square-Summable Steps Do Not Imply Finite Length

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connected Cluster-Set Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongest generic cluster-set conclusion from boundedness and asymptotic regularity in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((x^k)\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\), then its cluster set is nonempty, compact, and connected. It need not be a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded sequence with vanishing increments has a compact connected cluster set but need not converge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cluster set is nonempty, compact, and connected, but may contain more than one point.
knowledge_statements.title: Connected Cluster-Set Boundary
Failure Outside Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing steps and criticality residuals do not alone imply convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(F(x)=0\), represented by \(g=h=0\), and define
\[
x^k=(\cos(\log(k+1)),\sin(\log(k+1))).
\]
Then \(F(x^{k+1})=F(x^k)\), \(0\in\partial g(x^k)\cap\partial h(x^k)\), and \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\). Nevertheless, \((x^k)\) does not converge and has the unit circle as its cluster set. Thus monotonic objective values, exact criticality, and asymptotic regularity do not ensure sequential convergence without finite length, isolation, or another regularity mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slowly rotating sequence on the unit circle has zero residual and vanishing steps but does not converge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0\) and the residual is zero, but \((x^k)\) does not converge.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample content kind exactly fits the failure leaf, and the construction plausibly has vanishing increments, zero criticality residual, nonconvergence, and the unit circle as cluster set. It is nevertheless unsupported by a citation or explicit standard-field rationale, as required for candidate evidence.

children.title: DC Failure-Scope Boundary Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Failure modes are consolidated after the positive theory and kept distinct from application surveys owned by other chapters.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Stationarity, error-bound, and constrained-program distinctions in Chapters 6 and 8
Representation nonuniqueness and regularity topics in Chapters 3–5

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Augmentation Monotonicity and Smooth Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise effect of adding one finite convex function to both components of a finite DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g,h,\phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex functions and write \(f=g-h=(g+\phi)-(h+\phi)\). Then
\[
\partial g(x)\cap\partial h(x)\ne\varnothing\Longrightarrow \partial(g+\phi)(x)\cap\partial(h+\phi)(x)\ne\varnothing.
\]
If \(\phi\) is differentiable at \(x\), the implication is an equivalence. Thus a common nonsmooth augmentation may enlarge the decomposition-critical set, whereas a common augmentation differentiable at the point preserves criticality there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common convex augmentation cannot remove decomposition-critical points. It preserves criticality where it is differentiable but may create additional critical points at its nonsmooth points.
assumptions_latex: \(g,h,\phi\) are finite convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{crit}(g,h)\subseteq\operatorname{crit}(g+\phi,h+\phi)\), with pointwise equivalence wherever \(\phi\) is differentiable.

notation.meaning: critical set associated with the ordered DC decomposition

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Augmentation Monotonicity and Smooth Invariance
Decomposition-Dependent Critical Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC criticality can change when the same objective receives a different decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). For the decomposition \(f=g_1-h_1\) with \(g_1(x)=x^2\) and \(h_1(x)=0\), the condition \(\partial g_1(x)\cap\partial h_1(x)\ne\varnothing\) holds only at \(x=0\). Fix \(a=1/4\) and instead set
\[
g_2(x)=x^2+|x-a|,
\qquad h_2(x)=|x-a|.
\]
At \(x=a\), \(\partial g_2(a)=[-1/2,3/2]\) and \(\partial h_2(a)=[-1,1]\), so \(a\) is critical for the second decomposition although \(a\ne0\) is not a minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same convex kink to both DC components creates a new decomposition-critical point without changing the objective.
assumptions_latex: DC criticality means intersection of the two convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The critical set is \(\{0\}\) for \((g_1,h_1)\), but contains \(a=1/4\) for \((g_2,h_2)\).

notation.meaning: nonminimal kink location, equal to one quarter
two convex decompositions of the same objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample content kind fits the decomposition-dependence failure leaf. The displayed subdifferentials are internally consistent and show that adding the same convex kink changes the decomposition-critical set without changing f. However, the record has no citation or explicit standard-field rationale, so it lacks admissible evidence.

assumptions_latex: Work on \(\mathbb{R}\) with the DC decomposition \(f=g-h\).
Let \(g(x)=x^4+1\) and \(h(x)=2x^2\), both convex and differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(\bar x=0\) satisfies DC criticality but is not a local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth one-dimensional example separating DC criticality from local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=g(x)-h(x)=(x^2-1)^2\), DC criticality at \(\bar x\) means \(\partial g(\bar x)\cap\partial h(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\). At \(\bar x=0\), one has \(\partial g(0)=\partial h(0)=\{0\}\), so the criticality condition holds. Nevertheless, for every \(x\) satisfying \(0<|x|<1\), \(f(x)=1-2x^2+x^4<f(0)=1\). Hence \(0\) is a strict local maximizer and therefore is not a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC-critical point can be nonminimal: zero is critical for the displayed quartic DC decomposition but is a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical but Nonminimal Points

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary quartic counterexample is mathematically consistent, all TeX commands are delimited, and counterexample is the correct content kind for this failure leaf. However, no source reference or inspectable locator is supplied, so the claim cannot pass source review.

assumptions_latex: Use DC criticality \(\partial g(\bar x)\cap\partial h(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\) and directional stationarity \(f'(\bar x;d)\geq0\) for every \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(0\) is DC-critical for the chosen decomposition but is not directionally stationary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional nonsmooth example distinguishing decomposition criticality from directional stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=g-h=-|x|\). At \(\bar x=0\), \(\partial g(0)=[-1,1]\) and \(\partial h(0)=[-2,2]\), so \(\partial g(0)\cap\partial h(0)=[-1,1]\neq\varnothing\); thus \(0\) is DC-critical. For every nonzero direction \(d\), however, the directional derivative exists and equals \(f'(0;d)=-|d|<0\). Therefore the directional-stationarity inequalities fail in every nonzero direction, despite DC criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minus the absolute value, zero is critical under the displayed DC decomposition yet has a negative directional derivative in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical but Non-Directionally-Stationary Points

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subdifferentials and directional derivative are stated correctly, and the counterexample exactly separates decomposition criticality from directional stationarity. No supporting source or specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle and Subproblem Tractability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic usability requirements for an explicit DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an explicit decomposition \(f=g-h\), a standard exact DCA step requires both a computable selection \(y^k\in\partial h(x^k)\) and a computable solution of
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{g(x)-\langle y^k,x\rangle\}.
\]
The algebraic fact that \(g\) and \(h\) are convex does not ensure either operation is available or tractable. If the selected decomposition lacks one of these two oracles, it is a valid DC representation but does not define an implementable exact DCA iteration without approximation or a different decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid DC decomposition is algorithmically usable by exact DCA only when a subgradient of the subtracted component and a solution of the convex component subproblem can actually be computed.
assumptions_latex: \(f=g-h\) is an explicit DC decomposition with proper convex components.
Exact DCA is intended, rather than an independently specified inexact oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of either the \(\partial h\)-selection oracle or the convex minimization oracle makes the decomposition unusable for exact DCA.

notation.meaning: selected subgradient of the subtracted convex component

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle and Subproblem Tractability Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Component-Conditioning Bound for Smooth DCA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise conditioning of the exact smooth-DCA update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g,h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable convex functions, let \(g\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex, and let \(\nabla h\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Wherever the exact DCA map is defined by
\[
T(x)=(\nabla g)^{-1}(\nabla h(x)),
\]
it satisfies
\[
\|T(x)-T(z)\|\le \frac{L}{\mu}\|x-z\|.
\]
Hence \(L<\mu\) certifies contraction, while the guarantee degenerates as \(L/\mu\uparrow1\), even when cancellation leaves the represented difference well conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact smooth-DCA update has Lipschitz modulus at most the ratio of the second component's gradient-Lipschitz constant to the first component's strong-convexity modulus. Near unit ratio, the component-based rate guarantee degenerates.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
The displayed exact DCA update is defined at the points considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(T)\le L/\mu\); in particular, \(L/\mu<1\) certifies linear contraction.

notation.meaning: strong-convexity modulus of the first component
gradient-Lipschitz constant of the second component

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Conditioning Bound for Smooth DCA

assumptions_latex: Apply exact DCA by choosing \(y^k=\nabla h_M(x^k)\) and minimizing \(g_M(x)-y^kx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(g_M-h_M=x^2\) is independent of \(M\), the DCA contraction factor approaches \(1\) as \(M\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature cancellation makes an equivalent DC decomposition arbitrarily poorly conditioned for DCA.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every member of the family represents the same objective, since \(g_M(x)-h_M(x)=x^2\). The DCA relations are \(y^k=2Mx^k\) and \(x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\{(M+1)x^2-y^kx\}\), which give \(x^{k+1}=\frac{M}{M+1}x^k\). Consequently, reducing \(|x^k|\) by a fixed factor requires an iteration count growing on the order of \(M\). Thus large cancelling convex curvatures can make a valid decomposition arbitrarily ill-conditioned even when the represented objective remains fixed and simple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent decompositions of the same quadratic can make exact DCA arbitrarily slow because their large convex curvatures nearly cancel.
knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned or Intractable Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The DCA recurrence and asymptotic slowdown are internally correct, and failure_boundary fits the ill-conditioning leaf. The record nevertheless lacks a relevant source with an inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: Use exact DCA with \(y^k=\nabla h(x^k)\) and \(x^{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{g(x)-y^kx\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x^0\neq0\), the DCA trajectory is unbounded.

notation.meaning: selected subgradient of the subtracted convex term

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact DCA can escape when the DC objective lacks a lower-bounded level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective is \(f(x)=g(x)-h(x)=-\tfrac12x^2\), which is unbounded below. Exact DCA gives \(y^k=2x^k\), while the unique convex-subproblem minimizer satisfies \(x^{k+1}=y^k=2x^k\). Hence \(x^k=2^kx^0\). If \(x^0\neq0\), then \(|x^k|\to\infty\), showing that exact subproblem solution alone does not ensure bounded DCA trajectories without coercivity, bounded level sets, or another boundedness mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact DCA doubles every nonzero iterate for an unbounded-below quadratic DC objective, producing an unbounded trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded DCA Trajectories

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact DCA calculation correctly yields an unbounded trajectory for every nonzero initial point, and counterexample fits the terminal container. No source citation or locator supports the example or its stated failure scope.

assumptions_latex: Permit any minimizer of each DCA convex subproblem to be selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid exact-minimizer selection can generate the nonconvergent two-cycle \(1,-1,1,-1,\ldots\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique exact convex subproblems permit oscillation under an unrestricted selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every iteration, the selected subgradient is \(y^k=0\), and the DCA subproblem is \(x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\delta_{[-1,1]}(x)=[-1,1]\). Choose \(x^{k+1}=(-1)^{k+1}\). Every iterate is then an exact subproblem minimizer and the objective value is constantly \(0\), but the sequence alternates between \(-1\) and \(1\). Thus objective descent and exact solution do not yield iterate convergence when nonunique subproblems lack a consistent selection mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every point of an interval solves each exact DCA subproblem, alternating endpoint selections create a persistent two-cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique-Subproblem Oscillation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonunique subproblem admits the displayed alternating exact-minimizer selection, and counterexample is the appropriate knowledge kind. A source and specific locator are absent; a sourced version should also state the initialization explicitly when presenting the full two-cycle.

children.title: Nontrivial Cluster Sets Without Sequential Convergence

assumptions_latex: Choose exact DCA subproblem minimizers without a uniqueness or selection constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a bounded exact DCA sequence whose cluster set is \(\{-1,1\}\), although the sequence does not converge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness and constant objective values need not imply sequential convergence of DCA iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each DCA subproblem has the exact solution set \([-1,1]\). Select \(x^{2j}=1\) and \(x^{2j+1}=-1\) for every integer \(j\geq0\). The even subsequence converges to \(1\), the odd subsequence converges to \(-1\), and no other subsequential limits occur. Therefore \(\omega(x^k)=\{-1,1\}\), while \(\{x^k\}\) itself has no limit. This separates convergence of subsequences and objective values from convergence of the full iterate sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded exact DCA sequence may alternate forever, with two cluster points and no limit of the full sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Nontrivial Cluster Sets Without Sequential Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The alternating sequence has exactly the stated two-point cluster set and does not converge, matching the leaf and the counterexample content kind. No relevant citation or inspectable locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform nonvanishing error allowance can admit a bounded, nonconvergent inexact DCA sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonvanishing objective-gap tolerance is insufficient for convergence of inexact DCA iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact DCA subproblem has the unique solution \(0\) and optimal value \(0\). Set \(\varepsilon_k=\tfrac12\) and choose \(x^{k+1}=(-1)^{k+1}\). Then \(g(x^{k+1})=\tfrac12=\inf_x g(x)+\varepsilon_k\) at every iteration, so every step satisfies the stated inexactness test. Nevertheless, the iterates oscillate and never approach the exact solution. Thus a bounded but nonvanishing error sequence provides insufficient control; convergence results require stronger conditions such as vanishing, summable, or relative errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed positive subproblem tolerance allows alternating inexact iterates even though every exact DCA subproblem has the unique solution zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient Inexactness Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-tolerance counterexample is mathematically correct and fits the failure leaf. No source is supplied, and the closing reference to vanishing, summable, or relative errors requires sourced hypotheses because such error conditions are not sufficient in isolation for every inexact DCA variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Acceptance Classification for Boosting Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local availability and acceptance classification for a proposed boosting direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be Hadamard directionally differentiable at a DCA trial point \(z\), and consider boosted trials \(z+\lambda d\) with \(\lambda>0\). If \(d=0\), every trial equals \(z\), so boosting is unavailable. If \(d\ne0\) and \(f'(z;d)<0\), then for every \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), all sufficiently small \(\lambda>0\) satisfy
\[
f(z+\lambda d)\le f(z)+\sigma\lambda f'(z;d).
\]
If \(f'(z;d)>0\), all sufficiently small positive trials increase \(f\) and fail even objective nonincrease. When \(f'(z;d)=0\), first-order directional information alone is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero direction makes boosting unavailable; a negative directional derivative guarantees acceptance of sufficiently small Armijo boosts; a positive derivative guarantees local rejection; and a zero derivative requires higher-order information.
assumptions_latex: Boosted trials have the form \(z+\lambda d\) with \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=0\) is unavailable; \(f'(z;d)<0\) gives eventual Armijo acceptance; \(f'(z;d)>0\) gives local rejection; \(f'(z;d)=0\) is undecided at first order.

notation.meaning: Hadamard directional derivative at the trial point

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Acceptance Classification for Boosting Directions

assumptions_latex: Let \(g(x)=x^4+1\), \(h(x)=2x^2\), and initialize exact DCA at \(x^0=0\).
Define the boosting direction by \(d^k=z^k-x^k\), where \(z^k\) is the DCA subproblem solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At the nonminimal DC-critical point \(0\), the boosting direction is identically zero and no positive boost can be taken.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A DCA-displacement boost cannot leave a nonminimal fixed point when its direction vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x^k=0\), the selected gradient is \(y^k=\nabla h(0)=0\). The convex DCA subproblem therefore gives \(z^k=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\{x^4+1-y^kx\}=0\). Consequently \(d^k=z^k-x^k=0\), so every boosted trial point \(z^k+\lambda d^k\), with \(\lambda\geq0\), equals \(0\). Yet \(0\) is not a local minimizer of \(g-h\). Thus displacement-based boosting is unavailable at this critical fixed point unless an independent escape direction is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonminimal DCA fixed point, the usual displacement direction can vanish, leaving every boosted trial point unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Unavailable or Failed Boosting Directions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For the explicitly defined displacement-based boost, the zero direction calculation is correct and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The relevant boosted-DCA variant and its trial rule have no supporting source or specific locator.

children.title: Inertial Instability
children.top_down_role: Instability attributable to momentum or inertial terms in DC iterations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Scalar Additive-Inertia Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stability classification for additive momentum applied to a scalar DCA contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0<q<1\). The quadratic DC decomposition
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12x^2-\tfrac q2x^2
\]
has exact DCA map \(T(x)=qx\). For \(\beta\ge0\), consider the additive-inertia iteration
\[
x^{k+1}=T(x^k)+\beta(x^k-x^{k-1}).
\]
Every trajectory converges to \(0\) if and only if \(\beta<1\). At \(\beta=1\), the characteristic roots have product one and generic trajectories fail to converge to \(0\); for \(\beta>1\), an expanding characteristic mode exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additive inertia preserves convergence of a scalar exact-DCA contraction exactly for inertial weights below one.
assumptions_latex: The base exact-DCA map is generated by the displayed quadratic DC decomposition.
Momentum is added after evaluating the base map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\to0\) for every initial pair if and only if \(\beta<1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Scalar Additive-Inertia Boundary

assumptions_latex: Let the unaccelerated scalar iteration be \(x^{k+1}=qx^k\) with \(0<q<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inertial recurrence has an unstable mode although the underlying fixed-point iteration is contractive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excessive inertial weight destabilizes an otherwise contractive scalar update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The characteristic polynomial of the inertial recurrence is \(p(r)=r^2-(q+\beta)r+\beta\). Its two roots have product \(\beta>1\), so at least one root has modulus strictly greater than \(1\). Initial conditions with a nonzero component in the corresponding mode therefore fail to converge to \(0\), and generically their magnitudes grow without bound. Hence contractivity of the base update does not by itself control an inertial modification; the inertial parameter must satisfy an additional stability restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inertial weight above one introduces an expanding mode into a scalar contraction, so generic accelerated iterates fail to converge.
knowledge_statements.title: Inertial Instability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The characteristic-root argument correctly identifies instability when beta is greater than one, and failure_boundary is suitable. The recurrence is presented as a generic scalar fixed-point model without a source connecting it to the inertial DC/DCA context of the terminal container.

children.title: Extrapolation Instability
children.top_down_role: Instability attributable to extrapolated trial points or states.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Scalar Extrapolation Stability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stability classification for extrapolating the state before applying a scalar DCA contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0<q<1\). The quadratic DC decomposition
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12x^2-\tfrac q2x^2
\]
has exact DCA map \(T(x)=qx\). For \(\alpha\ge0\), consider
\[
z^k=x^k+\alpha(x^k-x^{k-1}),\qquad x^{k+1}=T(z^k).
\]
Every trajectory converges to \(0\) if and only if \(q\alpha<1\). At \(q\alpha=1\), the characteristic roots have unit modulus and generic trajectories do not converge to \(0\); for \(q\alpha>1\), an expanding characteristic mode exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extrapolating the state before a scalar exact-DCA contraction is stable exactly when the product of the contraction and extrapolation parameters is below one.
assumptions_latex: The exact DCA map is generated by the displayed quadratic DC decomposition.
The extrapolated state is evaluated by \(T(x)=qx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\to0\) for every initial pair if and only if \(q\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Scalar Extrapolation Stability Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extrapolation makes the contractive map unstable whenever \(q\alpha>1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation at an over-extrapolated point can destabilize a contractive update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extrapolated iteration obeys \(x^{k+1}=q(1+\alpha)x^k-q\alpha x^{k-1}\). Its characteristic roots have product \(q\alpha\). If \(q\alpha>1\), at least one root has modulus greater than \(1\), so suitable initial pairs generate nonconvergent, and generically unbounded, iterates. The boundary shows that applying a contractive map after extrapolation is not automatically contractive as a two-step method; stability requires control of the combined quantity \(q\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over-extrapolation destabilizes a scalar contraction once the product of contraction and extrapolation parameters exceeds one.
knowledge_statements.title: Extrapolation Instability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-step recurrence and instability condition q alpha greater than one are correct, and failure_boundary matches the leaf. No citation or locator establishes the intended extrapolated DC/DCA variant or its relevance to this taxonomy.

children.title: Parameter-Induced Oscillation
children.top_down_role: Oscillatory behavior associated with aggressive inertial or extrapolation parameters.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Relaxation-Induced Oscillation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact oscillation and divergence thresholds for relaxing a scalar DCA contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0\le q<1\), so the quadratic DC decomposition
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12x^2-\tfrac q2x^2
\]
has exact DCA map \(T(x)=qx\). For \(\lambda>0\), consider
\[
x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda(T(x^k)-x^k)
      =\bigl(1-\lambda(1-q)\bigr)x^k.
\]
Every trajectory converges to \(0\) when \(0<\lambda<2/(1-q)\). At \(\lambda=2/(1-q)\), every nonzero trajectory is a two-cycle. For \(\lambda>2/(1-q)\), every nonzero trajectory diverges geometrically with alternating signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing a scalar exact-DCA contraction is stable below a sharp parameter threshold, cycles at the threshold, and diverges with alternating signs above it.
assumptions_latex: The base exact-DCA map is generated by the displayed quadratic DC decomposition.
The update uses constant relaxation parameter \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact oscillation boundary is \(\lambda=2/(1-q)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Relaxation-Induced Oscillation Boundary

assumptions_latex: Let the base fixed-point map be \(T(x)=0\) on \(\mathbb{R}\).
Use the relaxed update \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda(T(x^k)-x^k)\) with constant \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The choice \(\lambda=2\) causes a two-cycle, while \(\lambda>2\) causes alternating divergence for every \(x^0\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Over-relaxation crosses a sharp oscillation boundary even for an exact constant update map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relaxed recurrence reduces to \(x^{k+1}=(1-\lambda)x^k\), hence \(x^k=(1-\lambda)^kx^0\). For \(0<\lambda<2\), every trajectory converges to \(0\). At \(\lambda=2\), every nonzero trajectory alternates between \(x^0\) and \(-x^0\). For \(\lambda>2\), the signs alternate and \(|x^k|=(\lambda-1)^k|x^0|\to\infty\). Thus \(\lambda=2\) is the exact scalar boundary between stable relaxation and parameter-induced oscillatory instability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation is stable below two, forms a two-cycle at two, and diverges with alternating signs above two.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Induced Oscillation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar relaxation boundary at lambda equal to two is calculated correctly and illustrates parameter-induced oscillation. The record has no source or inspectable locator connecting this generic relaxed fixed-point rule to the local DC-type optimization context.

children.title: Safeguard Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where restart, acceptance, or damping safeguards provide insufficient control.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Decrease Implies Asymptotic Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Control supplied by a positive displacement-dependent decrease safeguard and absent from nonincrease alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be bounded below along \((x^k)\). If every accepted step satisfies
\[
f(x^{k+1})\le f(x^k)-c\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2
\quad(c>0),
\]
then
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2
\le \frac{f(x^0)-\inf_k f(x^k)}{c}<\infty,
\qquad
\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\to0.
\]
Mere objective nonincrease, corresponding to \(c=0\), gives neither conclusion and cannot by itself exclude an equal-value cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive quadratic sufficient decrease makes accepted displacements square summable and hence vanishing. Objective nonincrease alone supplies no such anti-cycling certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below along the accepted iterates.
A uniform constant \(c>0\) appears in the acceptance test.
knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient Decrease Implies Asymptotic Regularity

assumptions_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) and consider the trial rule \(x^{k+1}=-x^k\).
Suppose a safeguard accepts every trial satisfying only \(f(x^{k+1})\leq f(x^k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonincrease-only safeguard accepts a nonconvergent two-cycle; any positive quadratic sufficient-decrease test rejects it away from \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mere objective nonincrease cannot exclude cyclic accelerated steps with unchanged objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x^k\), the trial satisfies \(f(x^{k+1})=f(-x^k)=f(x^k)\), so the nonincrease safeguard always accepts it. If \(x^0\neq0\), the accepted sequence alternates between \(x^0\) and \(-x^0\) and does not converge. By contrast, a test requiring \(f(x^{k+1})\leq f(x^k)-c|x^{k+1}-x^k|^2\) for some \(c>0\) rejects every such nonzero trial, because its left objective decrease is zero while \(|x^{k+1}-x^k|^2=4|x^k|^2>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeguard based only on nonincrease accepts an equal-value two-cycle, whereas positive sufficient decrease rejects every nonzero cycling step.
knowledge_statements.title: Safeguard Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-value two-cycle is accepted by the stated nonincrease test and rejected by the stated positive sufficient-decrease test, so failure_boundary fits the leaf. The safeguard model and its DC-acceleration relevance are unsupported by any source or specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Armijo Parameters Do Not Alone Certify Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Armijo scale near a stationary point and the diagnostic limit of using step parameters alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=x^2\), \(x_k>0\), \(d_k=-1\), and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\). The Armijo condition
\[
f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\le f(x_k)+\sigma\alpha f'(x_k)d_k
\]
holds for \(\alpha>0\) exactly when
\[
0<\alpha\le2(1-\sigma)x_k.
\]
Consequently accepted parameters must vanish if \(x_k\downarrow0\), although the iterates approach the stationary minimizer. Vanishing Armijo parameters by themselves therefore do not distinguish pathological line-search stagnation from ordinary convergence under normalized directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Armijo parameters can vanish normally as iterates approach a minimizer, so parameter decay alone is not a certificate of pathological stagnation.
assumptions_latex: \(\sigma\in(0,1)\) and the standard differentiable Armijo inequality is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\alpha_k\le2(1-\sigma)x_k\); thus \(x_k\downarrow0\) forces \(\alpha_k\to0\) without implying nonstationary stagnation.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Armijo Parameters Do Not Alone Certify Stagnation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Armijo Stagnation at a Nonstationary Point under Non-Gradient-Related Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth convex example where geometric Armijo backtracking accepts vanishing parameters and converges to a nonstationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x,y)=x+y^2/2\), choose \(\sigma\in(3/4,1)\), \( eta\in(0,1)\), and set \(c=4(1-\sigma)\in(0,1)\). At \(z_k=(x_k,y_k)\), where \(y_k>0\), take \(d_k=(-y_k,-1)\), and let \(\alpha_k\) be the largest element of \(\{1, eta, eta^2,\ldots\}\) satisfying \[f(z_k+\alpha d_k)\le f(z_k)+\sigma\alpha\langle
abla f(z_k),d_kangle.\] For all sufficiently small \(y_k\), this is equivalent to \(0<\alpha\le cy_k\), so \[ eta cy_k<\alpha_k\le cy_k.\] Therefore \(y_k\downarrow0\) geometrically, \(x_k\) converges, and \(\alpha_k	o0\), while the limit \(( ar x,0)\) is nonstationary because \(
abla f( ar x,0)=(1,0)
e0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a smooth convex objective, Armijo backtracking can converge with vanishing parameters to a nonstationary point when directions lose gradient-relatedness.
assumptions_latex: \alpha_k\text{ is chosen by geometric Armijo backtracking from }1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_k\to0,\qquad z_k\to(\bar x,0),\qquad\nabla f(\bar x,0)=(1,0)\ne0.
knowledge_statements.title: Armijo Stagnation at a Nonstationary Point under Non-Gradient-Related Directions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-Related Directions and Lipschitz Gradients Exclude Vanishing Armijo Steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard smooth boundary separating genuine stagnation from well-globalized descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on a neighborhood containing every trial segment, and suppose \[\langle\nabla f(x_k),d_k\rangle\le-\gamma\|d_k\|^2\] for some \(\gamma>0\). For \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), every \[0<\alpha\le\frac{2(1-\sigma)\gamma}{L}\] satisfies Armijo decrease. Thus geometric backtracking from a fixed \(\bar\alpha>0\), with factor \(\beta\in(0,1)\), accepts \[\alpha_k\ge\beta\min\left\{\bar\alpha,\frac{2(1-\sigma)\gamma}{L}\right\}>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform gradient-relatedness and Lipschitz-gradient control give a positive lower bound on accepted Armijo parameters.
assumptions_latex: \nabla f\text{ is }L\text{-Lipschitz on every trial segment}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_k\alpha_k\ge\beta\min\{\bar\alpha,2(1-\sigma)\gamma/L\}>0.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the gradient on trial segments

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Related Directions and Lipschitz Gradients Exclude Vanishing Armijo Steps
Line-Search Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing accepted steps in Armijo-backtracked descent for a nonsmooth DC objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|^p\) on \(\mathbb R\), where \(1<p<2\), and take \(x_k>0\) with \(x_k\downarrow0\) and steepest-descent directions \(d_k=-p x_k^{p-1}\). For an Armijo parameter \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), any accepted step crossing or approaching the kink must satisfy a scale restriction \(\alpha_k=O(x_k^{2-p})\). Hence \(\alpha_k\to0\), although \(d_k\neq0\) and every iterate outside the origin is nonstationary. Thus line-search globalization can stagnate through vanishing step lengths when no uniform sufficient-descent or curvature bound holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Armijo steps can vanish near a nonsmooth point even with nonzero descent directions; uniform descent or curvature control is needed to exclude this stagnation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k=O(x_k^{2-p})\to0\)

notation.meaning: descent direction at the kth iterate

source_refs.locator: 2.5.1 Unconstrained problems: Armijo line search p. 89

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.1 Unconstrained problems: Armijo line search p. 89

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the cited locator does not establish this particular example or the asserted scale. Moreover, |x|^p with 1<p<2 is differentiable at the origin, so describing the origin as a kink or nonsmooth point is inaccurate. The Armijo inequality, backtracking grid, and meaning of an accepted step that crosses or approaches the origin must be specified before the O(x_k^{2-p}) conclusion can be reviewed reliably.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-Base-Point Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility preservation under inner affine linearization of DC inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_i,h_i\) be proper convex functions, let \(x^k\in\operatorname{dom}g_i\cap\operatorname{dom}h_i\), and choose \(v_i^k\in\partial h_i(x^k)\). If \(g_i(x^k)-h_i(x^k)\le 0\) for every \(i\), then \(x^k\) satisfies every convexified constraint \(g_i(x)-h_i(x^k)-\langle v_i^k,x-x^k\rangle\le 0\). Hence the pure inner-linearized constraint system is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible linearization point remains feasible for the standard inner DC linearization, so emptiness requires an originally infeasible base point or additional incompatible restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\in\bigcap_i\{x:g_i(x)-h_i(x^k)-\langle v_i^k,x-x^k\rangle\le0\}\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: selected subgradient of the subtracted convex constraint component

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Base-Point Preservation
Linearized-Subproblem Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An inner convexification of a feasible DC constraint may have no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the DC constraint \(g(x)-h(x)\le0\) on \(\mathbb R\), with \(g(x)=1\) and \(h(x)=x^2\). Its feasible set is \(\{x:|x|\ge1\}\), so the original problem is feasible. At \(x_k=0\), the convex function \(h\) has subgradient \(v_k=0\). Replacing \(h\) by its affine minorant gives the convexified constraint \(g(x)-h(x_k)-v_k(x-x_k)\le0\), namely \(1\le0\). The linearized subproblem is therefore infeasible, despite feasibility of the original DC constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible reverse-convex constraint can yield an empty inner linearization when expanded at an unsuitable point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:g(x)-h(x_k)-v_k(x-x_k)\le0\}=\varnothing\)

notation.meaning: chosen subgradient of the convex function h

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent and its content kind fits the failure leaf: the original constraint is feasible, while the stated affine minorization at x_k=0 produces the impossible constraint 1<=0. No source is supplied for the DC inner-linearization convention or the failure phenomenon, so source support is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak versus Strong Recovery at the Exact-Penalty Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies the exactness convention at the threshold in the scalar penalty counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the constrained solution set and \(M_\rho=\operatorname*{argmin}P_\rho\). Weak recovery requires \(S\subseteq M_\rho\), whereas strong recovery requires \(M_\rho=S\). In the deferred scalar example, at \(\rho=1\) one has \(S=\{0\}\) and \(M_1=[0,\infty)\). Thus weak recovery holds at the threshold, but strong recovery and feasibility of every penalized minimizer fail; both notions hold for \(\rho>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the threshold, the constrained solution is a penalized minimizer, but infeasible minimizers remain; strict inequality is needed only for full minimizer-set recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\{0\}\) is the solution set of the deferred seed's constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq M_1\) but \(M_1\ne S\), while \(M_\rho=S\) for \(\rho>1\).

notation.meaning: global minimizer set of the penalized objective

knowledge_statements.title: Weak versus Strong Recovery at the Exact-Penalty Threshold
Penalty-Parameter Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite penalty below the exactness threshold admits nonoptimal or infeasible behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{-x:x\le0\}\), whose unique solution is \(x=0\). Its hinge-penalized objective is \(P_\rho(x)=-x+\rho\max\{x,0\}\). If \(0\le\rho<1\), then \(P_\rho(x)=(\rho-1)x\to-\infty\) as \(x\to+\infty\). If \(\rho=1\), every \(x\ge0\), including infeasible points, minimizes \(P_\rho\). Only \(\rho>1\) makes every global minimizer of the penalized problem feasible and equal to the constrained solution. Penalty updating can therefore fail when it never crosses the exactness threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a simple inequality, penalties below the multiplier threshold are unbounded or possess infeasible minimizers; exactness begins only above that threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho\le1\) fails exactness, whereas \(\rho>1\) yields \(\operatorname*{argmin}P_\rho=\{0\}\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and threshold calculations are correct, and counterexample is an appropriate kind for this failure leaf. However, the record has no citation for the exact-penalty interpretation or threshold claim, so it cannot pass source review.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Qualification Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of MFCQ can prevent KKT multipliers from existing at a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{x:x^2\le0\}\). The feasible set is the singleton \(\{0\}\), so \(x^*=0\) is a global minimizer. The active constraint gradient is \(\nabla(x^2)|_{x=0}=0\); hence no direction \(d\) satisfies the Mangasarian--Fromovitz inequality \(\nabla(x^2)|_{x=0}d<0\). Moreover, KKT stationarity would require \(1+\lambda\,0=0\) for some \(\lambda\ge0\), which is impossible. Thus a minimizer need not admit a KKT certificate after the relevant constraint qualification is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singleton feasible set has a global minimizer, but its zero active gradient makes MFCQ fail and rules out every KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists\lambda\ge0:\ 1+\lambda\nabla c(x^*)=0\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abnormal Fritz John Multipliers under Qualification Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General multiplier boundary explaining why a local minimizer may retain only an abnormal certificate when constraint qualifications fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \[\min_x f(x)\quad	ext{subject to}\quad c_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p),\] with all functions continuously differentiable near a local minimizer \(x^*\). The Fritz John necessary condition gives multipliers \((\lambda_0,\lambda,\mu)
eq0\) such that \(\lambda_0\geq0\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\lambda_i c_i(x^*)=0\), and \[\lambda_0
abla f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i
abla c_i(x^*)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j
abla h_j(x^*)=0.\] A suitable constraint qualification excludes the abnormal case \(\lambda_0=0\). When only abnormal multipliers are available, normalization to \(\lambda_0=1\) is impossible, so KKT stationarity need not follow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a suitable constraint qualification, Fritz John multipliers may have zero objective multiplier and therefore cannot be normalized to a KKT certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is a feasible local minimizer of the finite-dimensional nonlinear program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constraint-qualification failure may permit \(\lambda_0=0\), so a Fritz John certificate need not yield KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal Fritz John Multipliers under Qualification Failure
Nonunique Quasidifferential Representatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasidifferential pairs are equivalence representatives rather than unique generalized derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a directionally differentiable function satisfies \(f'(x;d)=\max_{a\in A}\langle a,d\rangle+\min_{b\in B}\langle b,d\rangle\) for all \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), where \(A\) and \(B\) are nonempty compact convex sets. For every nonempty compact convex set \(C\), the pair \((A+C,B-C)\) gives the same directional derivative because its two additional support terms cancel. Consequently, quasidifferential representatives are generally nonunique; any criterion or algorithm depending on a particular pair must either be invariant under this equivalence or impose a normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a common compact convex set to one quasidifferential component and subtracting it from the other leaves every directional derivative unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B,C\subset\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty compact convex sets
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\max_{a\in A+C}\langle a,d\rangle+\min_{b\in B-C}\langle b,d\rangle\)

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of A and C
Minkowski sum of B and the reflection of C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated transformation (A+C,B-C) does preserve the directional-derivative representation under the given convention, and property is an appropriate content kind. No source is supplied for this quasidifferential convention, its equivalence relation, or the resulting nonuniqueness claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Directed or Codifferential Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unnormalized representatives can be unboundedly unstable while the modeled directional derivative remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the zero function on \(\mathbb R^n\), every pair \((C,-C)\) of nonempty compact convex sets represents the same directional derivative, since \(\max_{c\in C}\langle c,d\rangle+\min_{b\in-C}\langle b,d\rangle=0\) for all \(d\). Taking \(C_k=k\mathbb B\) produces representatives whose diameters and Hausdorff distances from \(\{0\}\) diverge, although the represented function and derivative are unchanged. Therefore stability of directed, quasi-, or codifferential models cannot be inferred from function stability without a representative-invariant metric or a bounded normalization rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero function has representatives of arbitrarily large diameter, so representative sets can diverge while the modeled derivative remains identically zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=0\) for all \(d\), while \(d_H(C_k,\{0\})=k\to\infty\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is valid for the displayed quasidifferential convention, and it does demonstrate unbounded representative instability. The final conclusion extends the example to directed and codifferential models without defining those models or citing a source that justifies the extension. Authoritative support and terminology-specific hypotheses are needed.

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Approximate Quasi-DC Criticality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative-wise vector cancellation need not characterize directional stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x\) on \(\mathbb R\). Its directional derivative has the quasidifferential representation \(A=[0,1]\), \(B=[0,1]\), because \(f'(x;d)=\max_{a\in A}ad+\min_{b\in B}bd=d\) for every \(d\). Nevertheless, \(0\in A+B\), so the representative-wise residual \(\inf\{|a+b|:a\in A,b\in B\}\) equals zero. Since \(f'(x;-1)=-1<0\), no point is directionally stationary. Thus approximate criticality based only on selecting nearly cancelling representatives can be spurious unless the residual is invariant under quasidifferential equivalence and encodes all directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasidifferential pair for the linear function has zero cancellation residual even though the function has a strict descent direction everywhere.

notation.meaning: lower and upper quasidifferential representatives under the stated convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The calculations for A=B=[0,1] are internally correct under the stated max-plus-min convention, and the example shows that the selected cancellation residual does not imply directional stationarity. Because quasidifferential criticality and residual conventions vary, a source identifying this residual and its intended status is necessary before accepting the failure claim.

children.title: Chapter-Boundary Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Application and global-solution theories are represented only as outward navigation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Criticality Does Not Certify Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chapter-boundary example separating decomposition-based criticality from global solution certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=x^2\), \(h(x)=2|x|\), and \(f=g-h\) on \(\mathbb R\). Both \(g\) and \(h\) are convex, and \[\partial g(0)=\{0\},\qquad \partial h(0)=[-2,2],\] so \(\partial g(0)\cap\partial h(0)\ne\varnothing\) and \(0\) is DC-critical for this decomposition. Nevertheless, \[f(x)=(|x|-1)^2-1,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=\{-1,1\},\] and hence \(0\) is not globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition-critical point can fail to be globally optimal, so local DC criticality is not a global solution certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial g(0)\cap\partial h(0)\ne\varnothing\quad\text{but}\quad0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{-1,1\}.

notation.meaning: DC criticality for the displayed decomposition

knowledge_statements.title: DC Criticality Does Not Certify Global Optimality
Global DC Optimization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC criticality is a local certificate and does not certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=g(x)-h(x)\) on \(\mathbb R\), with \(g(x)=x^4+1\) and \(h(x)=2x^2\); both components are convex. At \(x=0\), \(\partial g(0)=\partial h(0)=\{0\}\), so the standard DC criticality inclusion \(\partial h(0)\cap\partial g(0)\neq\varnothing\) holds. Yet \(f(0)=1\), whereas \(f(1)=f(-1)=0\), the global minimum. Therefore a local DC method terminating at a critical point does not solve the global DC problem; global guarantees require separate bounding, enumeration, relaxation, or branch-and-bound machinery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC-critical point can be a strict nonglobal point, so local DC termination does not supply a global optimization certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is DC-critical but \(0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=\{-1,1\}\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example is correct: both components are convex, zero is DC-critical for the displayed decomposition, and the global minimizers are -1 and 1. The failure-boundary kind fits the chapter-interface leaf, but no source supports the chosen DC-criticality convention or the claimed boundary between local and global DC optimization.

assumptions_latex: For every \(i=1,\ldots,m\), the functions \(g_i,h_i:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) are finite-valued convex functions
The functions \(r_+,r_-:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) are finite-valued convex functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample learning objectives inherit DC structure from finite-valued DC losses and regularizers.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Structured Learning via Statistics and Optimization p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,p\in\mathbb N\), let \(z_1,\ldots,z_m\) be observations, and let \(\lambda\ge0\). Suppose that, for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\), the sample loss satisfies \(\ell_i(w)=g_i(w)-h_i(w)\), and suppose that the regularizer satisfies \(r(w)=r_+(w)-r_-(w)\), where \(g_i,h_i,r_+,r_-:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) are finite-valued convex functions. Then the regularized empirical objective \(F(w)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\ell_i(w)+\lambda r(w)\) has the DC representation \(F(w)=G(w)-H(w)\), where \(G(w)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i(w)+\lambda r_+(w)\) and \(H(w)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m h_i(w)+\lambda r_-(w)\) are convex on \(\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite regularized empirical objective is DC when every sample loss and the regularizer are differences of finite-valued convex functions on the common parameter space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be any set of \(\{0,1\}\)-valued functions. knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear complementarity is equivalently encoded by componentwise minimum residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\). A vector \(x\) solves the nonlinear complementarity problem precisely when \(x\ge0\), \(F(x)\ge0\), and \(x_iF_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\). These conditions are equivalent to the nonsmooth residual system \(\min\{x_i,F_i(x)\}=0\) for all \(i\), where the minimum is componentwise. Consequently, complementarity models interface with nonsmooth and DC optimization through merit functions formed from this residual, while feasibility and stationarity of such merit formulations must not be confused without an exactness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity is equivalent to setting each componentwise minimum of the primal variable and its residual to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\iff \min\{x_i,F_i(x)\}=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,n)\)

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A compact-set variational inequality is represented exactly by its primal gap function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\). Define the primal gap \(G(x)=\max_{y\in K}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle\) for \(x\in K\). Then \(G(x)\ge0\), since \(y=x\) is admissible, and \(x\) solves the variational inequality \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in K\) if and only if \(G(x)=0\). Thus equilibrium computation can be transferred to constrained minimization of a nonnegative gap function, subject to preserving its exact zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact convex set, a point solves the variational inequality exactly when its nonnegative primal gap equals zero.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\iff G(x)=0\)

notation.meaning: solution set of the variational inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Affine Gap Functions Are DC
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An affine variational inequality on a compact polytope has a finite maximum-of-quadratics primal gap and an explicit DC representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact polytope, let \(F(x)=Mx+q\), and set \(\phi_j(x)=\langle Mx+q,x-v_j\rangle\). Then \(G(x)=\max_j\phi_j(x)\). For any \(\rho\ge0\) satisfying \(M+M^\top+\rho I\succeq0\),
\[
G(x)=\max_j\left(\phi_j(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\right)-\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2,
\]
so \(G\) is finite-valued and DC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine variational inequality on a compact polytope, the primal gap is a finite maximum of quadratics with an explicit DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x)=\max_j(\phi_j(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2)-\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\) is DC.

notation.meaning: quadratic gap expression associated with vertex \(v_j\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Minimum Residuals Have Explicit DC Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar affine complementarity residuals admit two equivalent finite-valued DC representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For affine functions \(a,b:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\),
\[
\min\{a(x),b(x)\}=a(x)-\max\{a(x)-b(x),0\}
=\frac12\bigl(a(x)+b(x)-|a(x)-b(x)|\bigr).
\]
In each expression the residual is a difference of finite convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of two affine functions is affine minus convex and therefore provides an explicit DC complementarity bridge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{a,b\}=a-\max\{a-b,0\}=\tfrac12(a+b-|a-b|)\) is DC.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Minimum Residuals Have Explicit DC Decompositions
DC Reformulation Bridges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine complementarity residuals possess explicit finite-dimensional DC decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For affine scalar functions \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\), the complementarity residual \(r(x)=\min\{a(x),b(x)\}\) has the DC representation \(r(x)=a(x)-\max\{a(x)-b(x),0\}\). Equivalently, \(r(x)=\tfrac12(a(x)+b(x)-|a(x)-b(x)|)\). The first terms are affine and the maximum or absolute-value term is convex. Hence a finite affine complementarity system can be expressed through DC residual equalities or a finite sum of squared residuals, although equivalence of stationary points requires additional exactness analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum residual for affine complementarity is affine minus convex, providing an explicit bridge to DC formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Chapter-Ownership Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates DC optimization of an explicitly reformulated equilibrium problem from equilibrium and complementarity theory itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \(S:=\{x\in C:0\in F(x)+N_C(x)\}\), where \(N_C(x)\) is the convex-analysis normal cone. Suppose that finite convex functions \(a_j,b_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), give the exact representation \(S=\{x\in C:a_j(x)-b_j(x)\leq0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite convex functions. Then minimizing \(f-g\) over \(S\) is a DC-constrained optimization model after this representation is fixed. Its DC structure alone implies neither that \(S\neq\varnothing\) nor any conclusion about equilibrium multiplicity or stability, and it does not justify complementarity-specific pivoting methods; those matters belong to equilibrium, variational-analysis, or complementarity theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once an equilibrium solution set has an exact finite DC-inequality representation, minimizing a DC objective over it is a DC-constrained model. DC structure alone does not establish equilibrium existence, multiplicity, or stability and does not justify complementarity-specific pivoting methods.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) has the displayed exact representation by finitely many DC inequalities.
\(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and all \(a_j,b_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are finite convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in S}\{f(x)-g(x)\}\) is a DC-constrained model, but its DC structure alone implies neither \(S\neq\varnothing\) nor equilibrium multiplicity or stability and does not supply complementarity-specific pivoting theory.

notation.meaning: convex-analysis normal cone to C at x

children.title: Sparse Optimization Interface
